models the verified control relationship without claiming the full fixed
controller state machine or all player transitions are complete.

The Stage 0 controller also calls `0xc33e`, but its jump-like transition is
gated by `a5+0x799e`, not a player button. The sampler reads `0x80001e`
and increments this flag only when the inverted DSWC mode bit 7 and bit 3 are
set. MAME identifies these as Test mode and the Test-mode Invulnerability
debug switch; its input map sends `0x800018`–`0x80001f` reads to the DIP banks
([MAME Willow DIP definition](https://github.com/mamedev/mame/blob/master/src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp#L1289),
[CPS-1 input map](https://github.com/mamedev/mame/blob/master/src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp#L531)).
When that debug flag is active and the controller record crosses the stored Y threshold,
`0xc33e` selects the `0xd27a` animation and initializes jump-like state. This
debug transition is separate from normal gameplay jumping. Routine
`0xc716` tests a newly pressed bit 5 before the normal controller branches to
`0xc434`; MAME's Willow input definition inherits the CPS-1 three-button
layout, where bit 5 is Button 2 ([MAME source](https://github.com/mamedev/mame/blob/master/src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp#L763)).
The fixed record initialized by `0x2f08` is active in Stage 0, and its
stage-counter-zero selector at `0x2f72` is 0. At `0xbf00`, that selector routes
to `0xbf42`; the alternate controller at `0xd4ba` is selected only for
selector 1. Reset clears the record's state bytes; its first dispatch follows
major state 0 at `0xbf42`, then substate 0 at `0xbf74`. The opening state waits
for the stage gate, runs a 16-tick timer, then advances to major state 2. The
state-2 table at `0xbf54` selects `0xc13e`; its substate-0 entry at `0xc164`
selects `0xc3b6`, which reaches normal input at `0xc400` after initialization.
The catalog validates this route and the shared-target comparison in
`build/willow_objects.json`. With Down clear, the Button 2 edge makes
`0xc434` set fixed-record +3 to 2. The next `0xc13e` dispatch indexes
`0xc164` at byte offset 2; word `0x0626` resolves to `0xc78a`. Its +4=0
entry launches at `0xc7bc`, and Up bit 3 selects `0x0580` instead of `0x0440`.
This computed path establishes the normal Stage 0 jump. The
native loop now preserves that one-update dispatch delay between the Button 2
edge and jump launch. The active Stage 0 controller therefore uses the
`0xc434` → `0xc78a` → `0xc7bc` route; the `0xdb30` → `0xdc0a` route belongs
only to the selector-1 controller and is not used by this actor.
`0xd4ba` path in major state 2, substate 0 reaches normal input at `0xdb00`; a
Button 2 edge at `0xc716` takes `0xdb30`, which sets substate 2 and clears the
next substate. On the following update, the `0xda8a` state table dispatches
substate 2 to `0xdbd6`, whose substate 0 selects launch handler `0xdc0a`.
That alternate handler sets vertical speed to `0x0440`, or `0x0580` when Up
bit 3 is held, applies launch movement, and runs `0x39fe`. It dispatches only
when its actor byte `+32` is 1. Stage 0 actor allocation `0xa2a6` sets
`+32 = 3` and dispatches to `0x125d0`; the Stage 0 fixed controller instead
uses `0xc3b6` and reaches the `0xc78a` jump dispatcher through the computed
state table. The separate direct-reference scan still finds no branch, call,
or literal pointer to `0xc78a`; that scan does not cover the validated runtime
table path. The object catalog validates each computed table and transition in
`build/willow_objects.json`.
The catalog also scans the assembled 68000 region for direct branches, calls,
jumps, PC-relative LEA references, and literal pointer words to `0xc78a`; none
are present. The active object handler table at `0xffc8` also does not contain
`0xc78a`; Stage 0 reaches it through the fixed controller's computed state
table. The controller route to `0xdc0a` is separately validated through its
computed state tables.
The generated header contains animation metadata and tile codes, not arcade
program code. The separately reverse-engineered generic enemy prototype uses
the source animation table `0x1116e`, selected by handler `0x1010e`. Its two
directional loops use the six source frame codes, 4x4 CPS tile blocks, and
six-tick holds. This prototype is currently disabled in the Stage 0 game path
because its native spawn has not been linked. Its native prototype state model uses the
source four-frame proximity cadence, seven-unit vertical approach steps, and
the center surface probe result from `0x3b0a` to enter its mirrored `0x11226` attack frames
with source durations and dimensions. Enemy frame timers now use the source
decrement-before-advance cadence, with the frame selected on each update
counted as its first visible tick. Its facing now follows the source
`0x10db4` comparison, including the left-facing flip when the enemy is right
of Willow. Changing its idle facing restarts that direction's loop at frame
zero. The charged dash animation also advances
during its source three-tick startup, while horizontal movement waits for that
startup to finish.
The native enemy reproduces the source approach cadence and enters state 8
substate 2 (`0x10962`) directly when the center surface probe succeeds. The
`0x11226` attack animation advances independently from its random check timer.
The main dispatcher at `0xffa2` calls each active actor handler once per frame.
The helper at `0x2244` only admits the actor to an in-range visibility queue
when its origin is within `x = -32..416` and `y = 0..272` relative to the
camera origin at `a5+0x408/+0x40c`; it also sets the actor's `+1` visibility
flag. Native actor culling now compares camera-relative screen coordinates.
The active class-2 enemy AI compares the moving shared controller target at
`a5+0x184c/+0x1850`, as its source routines do; the separate generic enemy
rendering prototype remains disabled, and its out-of-window timer pause is an approximation
that must be removed when a verified Stage 0 enemy spawn is connected.
The native code now ports the `0x1d8e` 16-bit LFSR recurrence and uses its
returned low byte to select the source's 32, 64, 96, or 128 tick interval.
The object catalog validates the helper's complete instruction bytes and
exports its taps and recurrence. The Stage 0 seed is generated into
`willow_score.h` from the first word (`0xf697`) in the two-record table at
`0x8cca`, and the runtime initializes its shared state from that constant.
The reset vector enters at `0x404`; startup clears 64 KiB
of work RAM at `0x6f2` and sets `a5` to `0xffff8000` at `0x5b6`. At `0x8cec`,
the 68000 brief address displacement `0x8e5a` is signed (`-0x71a6`), giving
effective address `0xffff0e5a`, or `0xff0e5a` on the 24-bit main bus. MAME's
CPS-1 main map exposes RAM at `0xff0000`–`0xffffff`
([MAME `main_map`](https://github.com/mamedev/mame/blob/master/src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp#L531-L548)), so reset clears this selector before Stage 0 setup.
Its zero value selects seed `0xf697`; setup copies that seed, then toggles the
selector at `0x8d54`. The other record contains `0xa649`.
Later LFSR parity also depends on matching every
intervening source draw and subsequent stage entry. A
successful timing check, or the ordinary no-special-collision return from
`0x10c9c`, enters state-8 substate 4. The native path now applies its three
source horizontal steps and shared center surface probes during the first
three ticks, advances through the fourth tick into substate 6, then begins the
state-8 substate-0 probe path after the one-tick substate-6 timer. That probe
logic evaluates the profile-6 directional Scroll 2 property
probe from `0x10864` at enemy X ±48 and enemy Y, then tests the bit-3 solid
probes at `(enemyX +/- 32, enemyY - 16)` and `(enemyX +/- 32, enemyY - 41)` in
source order. The solid-property helper follows `0x4074`: bit 3 must be set
and bit 2 clear, keeping one-way platform classes out of wall-contact branches.
The shared movement-surface probe follows `0x40a0`'s negative bit-6 secondary
tile check; it now propagates the first Y correction even when that second
check fails, while preserving the false contact result for state transitions.
After the recovery delay, the native loop also ports the above-target branch
of `0x10c9c`: within its 30-pixel vertical window it checks the enemy-center
points at Y +39, +55, +71, and +87, then re-enters the seven-pixel approach
state when any point has the source property. The below-target branch checks
Y -80, -96, -112, and -128, then enters state 6 and runs the source-ordered
directional and terrain probes on the next object update. The first source
frames from animation tables `0x113fa` and `0x11416` are exported with their
record durations, dimensions, and flips, packed into the uncompressed sprite
stream, and advanced independently of the helper's 16-tick object field. The
`0x113fa` sequences retain their 12-tick frames and 22-tick blank frame before
the long-delay control record; `0x11416` retains its 12-tick and four-tick
directional frames. The shared 18-byte record at `0x11416` uses descriptor word 3
(`0x3210`) and now resolves all four appended CPS components with the source
origin-template coordinates `(-16,-8)`, `(0,-8)`, `(-32,-16)`, and
`(-32,0)`. Its uncompressed Genesis atlas stores each 3x4 CPS component as
6x8 8x8 patterns. The atlas packs the 4x4 CPS components as four contiguous
4x4-pattern sprite blocks; the 3x4 components use contiguous 4x4, 2x4, 4x4,
and 2x4-pattern blocks. The renderer keeps the four component origins and
source horizontal flip. The native build and ROM audit pass; this frame has
not been visually compared against arcade output.
Both extended records occur at source frame indices `[2, 1]` in the two
directional sequences; the catalog now derives and exports those indices and
the renderer uses them to select the composed frame. A terminal-generated
source-versus-Genesis-block preview showed matching component layouts for
both compositions.
The related `0x11482` contact/setup frame is also composed from four 4x4 CPS
components using descriptor `0x3330` and origin template `0x0010`; its source
codes and resolved coordinates are emitted in `enemy_setup_composition` in
`build/willow_animations.json`.
The former 14x2 animation lead at `0x1493a` was a false
positive: `0x1493c-0x1494e` is executable code that copies object fields and
returns, not a CPS animation record. It is excluded from the native frame
catalog; additional valid special-animation tables still need discovery.
The helper's global event locks remain unported. The mode-4
below-target path also checks the extra solid point at Y -32 before the
four-point scan.
The randomized attack check now runs the same `0x10c9c` collision scan before
leaving state 8 substate 2. A matching above-target or below-target terrain
probe selects its corresponding special animation and state path; a miss
continues into the normal four-tick recovery sequence. The scan calls the
terrain-property helper at `0x3c40` and mutates the enemy state; this path does
not call Willow's hurt/knockback handler, so the attack pose is not evidence
of a player hit. The preceding `0x1098a` gate computes unsigned
`enemyY - sharedTargetY + 30` and calls the scan only when that value is at
least 60; the native class-2 branch now follows that comparison, and the
object catalog validates the source branch bytes. It now also validates the
four-iteration `0x10d60` loop byte-for-byte: each pass calls `0x3c40` with the
enemy X and one of four terrain Y samples, returning zero after four misses.
The scan's stage and
shared-gate checks are modeled; remaining
global event locks and later recovery states are still incomplete.
The source dispatcher routes above-player substate `+3=2` to `0x104e6`,
which uses the `0x114ba` entry stream and then the `0x114d6` rising stream.
The separate substate `+3=4` handler at `0x105de` uses the exact vector table
at `0x10636`: (+32/-32,+10), (0,+32), (0,+10), and (-8/+8,0), with eight-tick
holds and the source terminal terrain branch. The native runtime now keeps
these source substates distinct and exports the two additional frame streams.
Native enemy probes now preserve the source `ADDW`/`SUBW` coordinate wrapping
before the 12-bit map lookup at `0x3e28`, including the `0x3b0a` profile
points, its center correction, the state-8 scans, and the `Y-33` substate
probe, and the `0x3bc6` `X±2`/`Y-25` recovery contact when those points cross
a map edge. The `0x40a0` center correction now also wraps the 16-bit integer
Y word and clears the fractional word exactly as the source does.
Its negative-shape branch also bypasses the `0x3e4c` guard that rejects
heights of at least 9 when the Y fraction is below 7. The native helper keeps
the routines' distinct retry rules: `0x3e4c` retries either sign when bit 6 is
set, while `0x40a0` retries only negative bit-6 shapes. Each retry looks at
the original center probe plus the first correction and applies the retry
correction to actor Y only when the second probe succeeds. Native callers now
retain the first correction even when that retry returns no contact, matching
the source's in-place object-Y mutation before its zero return.
The `0x3bc6` recovery contact uses the second byte of the property record as
the Y threshold for collision classes 8 and 12, including its low five bits;
the native predicate now reads that shape byte instead of the flag byte.
The fixed-object handler `0x10054` has been statically traced through its
state-2 attack, animation, recovery, and collision routines. Those details
belong to the separate fixed-object pool and are not part of the Stage 0
charged class-2 runtime. The previous native simulation was incorrectly wired
to the charged pool; it is now bypassed for those records. The fixed-object
pool still needs its own native scheduler and actor lifecycle before these
traces can drive gameplay.

The source
helper at `0xc8a2` adds a fixed-point value read from
the object pointer at `fp+24` to vertical position; the pointer's role and the
states that consume that value still need to be mapped before reproducing it.

A near-probe hit selects state 12. The native state 12 path waits six ticks
after its +0x0380 setup, clears the velocity, then probes `0x3b0a` before each
one-step update. A miss applies the source -0x0028 velocity update down to
-0x0780 and seven-pixel terminal movement with the `0x20b4` X step and one
animation advance; a hit or set `+36` starts the four-tick tail. On each tail
tick, byte `+31` either returns early to state 8 or keeps
the `0x208c` motion, terrain probe, and animation update active; timer expiry
clears the substate. The shared `0x3b0a` collision model now clears and sets
native byte `+31` from the directional side probe while preserving the
distinct `+36` field tested before the probe. The movement phase continues the
inherited `0x11226` animation with source holds. A negative higher-probe shape
selects state 20. Its native path advances that animation, applies the
facing-specific 8.8 motion from the object's `0x115ce` velocity pair, and
repeats the shared side and center probes until side contact exits the state.
On exit, it compares facing with the enemy's side relative to Willow and,
when needed, plays the two-frame `0x1136e` return sequence for its source
eight-tick state-16 interval before restoring the probe path or directional
idle. Object scheduling effects remain approximated.

A nonnegative higher-probe shape selects state 14. That path now ports its
entry -0x0200 8.8 vertical velocity, then its per-tick animation advance,
shared side/center terrain probe, -0x0028 acceleration down to -0x0780, and
seven-pixel terminal movement. It applies the `0x20b4` facing-selected
horizontal delta after the vertical update. State 20 now performs its initial
`0x3b0a` probe on entry and consumes that side-hit result before advancing on
the next tick, matching the source branch order. It
continues the selected `0x11226` attack sequence with source frame holds
during knockback. Its exact state exit effects remain incomplete.
The state-8 timer expiry now calls the same target-relative scan as source
`0x10c9c` when its vertical range check fails, entering the matching above- or
below-player attack state when the terrain probes succeed. Other
`0x10962..0x109c6` interaction branches and player/enemy hit outcomes are not
yet ported. The
full object spawn scripts and multiple-enemy scheduling are also missing.
Enemy graphics stream uncompressed
into a separate VRAM range. The release omits the developer asset browser, so
Mode+Start cannot leave the game for the inspector. Developer builds made with
`make release ASSET_BROWSER=1` can use Mode+Start to open or close the tile
and audio browser. In the browser, up/down pages through
the packed animation-referenced sprite codes by source address, left/right
selects an OKI sample, A plays it, X toggles playback through the first source
command mapped to that sample, B stops it, and C steps through 32 converted
CPS palette groups. `tools/cps1_palette.py`
decodes the game's xRGB444 colors, applies the runtime `0xf000` brightness
initialization, and quantizes them for Genesis CRAM using MAME's color
conversion. Scroll layers use source pen zero as transparent. CPS sprites use
pen 15, so the native sprite
stream rotates source pens by one and the sprite palettes rotate colors to
keep opaque source pen zero visible. Willow's native poses select their
catalogued source color group on PAL0. The opening Stage 0 class-12 actor now
selects the source frame's color group on PAL1 (group 31), restoring the
default group 16 when it leaves the visibility window. The Stage 0 post-phase
actor sequence uses source group 8 on PAL1 while active. Other simultaneous
actors still share PAL1; catalogued class-2 behavior-0 actors also select
group 8 while visible. Palette selection for other source object fields is
incomplete. The native jump path is now connected to the verified Stage 0 Button 2 route. Its
modeled phases and remaining transition gaps are described below. Its ascent
pose `0xd27a` is selected by Stage 0 handler `0xc7bc` and reloaded by `0xc888`
when facing changes. Native rendering keeps that one-frame pose throughout the
modeled jump. Frames `0xd2ca/0xd2ce` belong to internal dispatcher `0xc8f2`,
which has no verified link to the Stage 0 actor. The alternate controller
launches through `0xdc0a`, with Up selecting `0x0580` instead of `0x0440`.
The native jump now follows the verified Stage 0 substates. After `0xc7bc`
initializes speed, `0xc7ec` moves by `+56`, checks `0x39fe`, and subtracts
player field `+52` (`0x0038`) until contact or zero speed advances to `0xc820`.
The native jump accumulator uses the source actor's 16.16 world-Y format;
each signed 8.8 velocity is shifted into that format before movement, and
collision corrections preserve the low fractional word.
That ascent handler subtracts speed from Y and adds `+52` until speed reaches
`0x0700`. Since `0x0700` is exactly 32 increments of `0x0038`, the terminal
value is `0x0700`. It exits on `0x38f6` contact or enters state 8 when the Up gated
`0xc57a` probe succeeds. Native code follows these transitions and keeps the
source-selected `0xd27a` pose. The separate `0xc8f2/0xc906/0xc9da` falling
path remains cataloged without a verified link to the Stage 0 actor; its
`0xd2ca/0xd2ce` frames are not used by this jump.
Holding Genesis A arms the primary-action charge on the first held update;
the source counter begins incrementing on the next held update. Release after
the counter reaches 16 starts the native burst, requiring the arm update plus
16 counter updates. This follows the input counter in `0xc610`, the
directional `0xd3be` three-frame pose selected at `0xcde8`, and the `0x0700`
horizontal speed reduced by `0x0040` per frame in `0xce24-0xce5c`. The terminal
`0xd3c2` pose is shown for six frames. Animation-table selection at burst entry
returns without a `0x1f4c` step, so native code skips frame-timer advancement on
that entry update; subsequent animation updates use the source six-tick holds.
Burst position now stays in stage
coordinates while the camera scrolls and is clamped to the Stage 0 world bounds.
Burst state entry at `0xcdf0` sets its startup timer to three and returns before
motion. The native action setup runs into its update block in that same frame,
so it seeds four and consumes one immediately, leaving the source's three full
countdown updates before the first movement frame.
On release after the counter reaches 16, the native preview now follows the source
charge-state timing at `0xca1c`: `0xd1a2` (or Down pose `0xd1aa`) for five
ticks, then `0xd1a6` (or `0xd1ae`) for five ticks. Facing, tile code, and
dimensions come from the four source animation tables. In Stage 0, mode
`a5+0x366` is set to 1 at `0x8d7e`. A 16-tick
charge indexes `0xcb08` at entry 2, then `0xcb4c` at entry 8, selecting
behavior index 1. The `0xcc50` table maps that to object byte `+32 = 1`; the
spawn writes byte `+33 = 1`, player X and facing, and player Y with an 8-pixel
offset unless the down flag is set. The primary child takes its record from queue class 8 through allocator
`0x2b04`. The class-8 scheduler at `0xe6f4` routes its `+32=1` behavior to
`0xec84`; that entry sets a 64-tick timer, enters state 2, installs the
`0xed0c` direction vectors, and selects an animation stream from `+33`. State 2
at `0xed7c` moves using byte `+15` at four pixels per tick and checks the
camera window every fourth global frame. Timer expiry or leaving that window
enters state 6, which returns the record through `0x2b20` to the class-8 LIFO
free list. Native code now follows the initial position, 64-tick lifetime,
horizontal vector, periodic camera cull, and LIFO allocation/cleanup. The
animation catalog validates the two facing streams at `0xf040`/`0xf074`:
four 2×2 CPS frames (`0x264`, `0x266`, `0x248`, `0x24a`) on three-tick holds,
with horizontal flip in the second stream. The native renderer uses these
records and their one-pixel X origin. Native collision handling mirrors
`0x3744`: a direct point hit enters state 4, plays the facing-specific four
frame impact stream from `0xf2ec`/`0xf320` on three-tick holds, then returns
through state 6 after 12 ticks. Four ordered side probes use offsets
`(+16,-16)`, `(+16,0)`, `(-16,-16)`, and `(-16,0)`; a successful directional
probe applies the source X-fraction correction and clears fractional X.
The native update orders timer expiry, periodic `0x2212` culling, movement,
animation, and collision as in `0xed7c`, allowing the later collision result to
replace an earlier state-6 expiry on the same tick.
The `0x115ee` patrol, proximity,
lunge, and voice route is a separate class-4 actor and is not used for this child.

The same held-charge handler has a second allocation path that is distinct
from the primary queue-class-8 child created on release. `0xc610` arms a 10-tick timer,
sets the active flag at +63, clears the charge counter at +49, and returns.
The counter increment and `0xc6c0` timer decrement begin on the next held-charge
update. The source reload table at `0xc706` is `[10, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 2, 1]`;
the native code consumes these validated values directly. Timer expiry attempts
a queue-class-2 allocation through `0x29d0` only while more than one record remains;
the new record is active type 1, has behavior byte `+32 = 0`, and receives
collision mode byte `+33` from the shared LFSR masked with 6. The reload table
is the same `0xc706` table: helper `0xc6f6` indexes it with charge counter
`+49 >> 4` each time the timer expires. Saturated charge separately sends cue
`0x44` on selected global-frame ticks. The spawn context writes no X/Y fields. State 0 in the active class-2
behavior-0 handler `0xfb7c` sets both coordinates around the shared Stage 0
target origin `(0,0)`, then consumes two more shared-LFSR draws for the offset
and timer. Native code now follows the 19-to-0 scheduler order,
sets the source 9/16/7/24-tick timer, counts down state 2, and returns the
record to its LIFO class-2 free pool in state 4. It does not run the separate
`0x10054` state machine. Updates to the shared target and the alternate offset
table remain to trace. The class-2 free routine at `0x29ec` preserves
coordinate history; state 0 overwrites both coordinates before the actor uses
them again. The object catalog validates the charge allocator, pool
dispatcher, and handler state table. The animation catalog now independently
checks the complete state-0 spawn/selector instructions at `0xfc10`, the
state-2 mode dispatch and visibility call at `0xfc6c`, and the lifetime/frame
update and cleanup tail at `0xfc84`. The checked source order is: state 0
draws twice from the shared LFSR, selects the lifetime and animation stream
with the second draw, then calls `0x1f30`; state 2 calls the mode callback and
`0x2244` before decrementing its lifetime and calling `0x1f4c`; state 4
returns the record through `0x29ec` on its next dispatch. The generated
catalog also byte-checks the `0x2244` visibility filter and records its
camera-relative bounds (`x=-32..416`, `y=0..272`), which match the native draw
window. These checks keep the native timer, animation, and visibility ordering
tied to the offline source image.
The release-time
class-2 behavior-1 child now returns its pool record after the source
eight-tick state. Linked children and other modeled class-2 records run in the
same descending record order, preserving their relative cleanup and free-list
updates. Unmodeled class-2 behavior selectors remain outside this dispatcher.
During ordinary play, the class-2 behavior-0 renderer now has a compact path
for more than four visible source records. It streams one uncompressed 16x16
frame per actor into a contiguous 4-pattern cache, draws the actors in the
source scheduler's 19-to-0 order, and reserves four patterns per additional
actor before the later caches. This supports all 20 pool records within the
current Stage 0 pattern budget. The post-phase composite keeps its existing
renderer to avoid cache overlap. Genesis scanline sprite limits can still hide
overlapping actors, and the expanded sprite ordering has not yet been compared
with arcade captures.

The fixed-object handler `0x10054` belongs to a separate 50-record, 128-byte
pool. Its source state and behavior tables are cataloged, but that pool's native
runtime is not implemented. The earlier native class-2 code incorrectly applied
parts of this handler to charged actors; charged behavior-0 records now bypass
that code and follow the 20-record scheduler at `0xfb48`.

For the Stage 0 charged class-2 records, native dispatch now runs in source
slot order 19 down to 0. The scheduler passes the physical slot number as
`d7` (`19 - zero-based slot index`), which the native runtime uses for the
staggered `(global frame + d7) & 15` checks. The scheduler instruction bytes
and LIFO free-list initialization are validated by the object catalog. State 0
uses the verified `0xfb90` offset table and
the two shared-LFSR draws, anchored at the normal Stage 0 target origin
`(0, 0)`, and selects the source 9/16/7/24-tick lifetime. The animation
catalog now follows all four animation streams selected by that second RNG
draw, exports their exact 16x16 CPS codes and holds, and checks the `0x1f30` /
`0x1f4c` walker instructions. On every state-2 update, the source decrements
the lifetime and enters state 4 at expiry, calls `0x1f4c` to advance animation,
then returns through visibility helper `0x2244`. The native actor follows that
order, advances when the selected frame hold reaches zero, and holds the
terminal source frame. State 4 returns the record to the native LIFO free
pool on the next scheduler update. The normal Stage 0 initializer leaves the
shared target at `(0, 0)` after work-area reset. The separate stage-counter-3
initializer at `0xa186` writes X=448 and does not apply to normal Stage 0
startup. Native Willow input starts at the normal-path coordinates and adds
the verified controller vectors each update. Later shared-target writes are
in the stage controller: `0xa466` sets target X to −32 while advancing
controller word `a5+8` and loading a 256-tick timer; `0xa57e` adds 8 to target
Y when `a5+0x1866` is nonzero while advancing the controller and loading a
63-tick timer. Their reachability during ordinary Stage 0 play is not
established; the alternate `0xfbd0` offset table is also not selected. The
object catalog validates the startup work-RAM clear, normal Stage 0 reset
helper, and the separate counter-3 write, so this target origin is checked
against the source reset and initializer bytes. The
former references to `0x2d8c6` and `0x30d40` were incorrect: those locations
are animation/state code, not writers to the shared target. The native renderer currently schedules at most four
simultaneous class-2 sprites. The class-2 behavior-1 child allocated at
`0xcc28` is linked to the same charge-release path: it is created only after
the queue-class-8 allocation at `0xcba6` succeeds. The native runtime models its
eight-tick target-relative animation and class-2 pool return; the separate
queue-class-8 64-tick movement lifecycle is not applied to it.

The sequenced cues are not direct OKI samples and still need the native YM/OKI
cue player.

Player handler `0x125d0` also has two source-backed actor creation paths, at
`0x12dfa` and `0x138ba`. Both queue sound command `0x34`, allocate selector 0
from queue class 10, and dispatch through `0x2359c`. The first places the actor
using the low nibble of player byte `+48`; the second derives its direction
from player byte `+15` and may subtract 16 from Y when byte `+46` is clear.
The first path is selected by player byte `+80`, requires the linked record at
`+38` to have byte `+60` set, and starts a 48-tick timer. The second actor has
two verified triggers: at `0x13762`, a precomputed range value minus `a5+0x040c`
must be below 144 before the handler selects facing and calls `0x138ba`; or the
16-tick player substate timer expires at `0x1383c`. The catalog validates both
trigger contexts, spawn sites, and the selector-0 table entry. The native
player now connects the first trigger when Stage 0 state-2 substate 0 enters
the less-than-144 Y window around the reset target. It uses the shared
selector-0 effect lifecycle and source X/Y offsets. This does not yet port the
player's full associated pose sequence or sequenced sound cue `0x34`. The
facing-specific first frame from `0x131b0` is now byte-validated and rendered
during the eight-tick entry phase, followed by the source six-frame
`0x13164` animation on its 48-tick timer. The next 16-tick substate allocates
the second selector-0 actor using separate native state and tile-cache slots,
so the two effects can overlap. The following 16-tick and 56-tick timers are
modeled. The source `0x13160` tail now renders all seven records, including
their facing, origin, dimensions, and six eight-tick advances; the last record
is held until the outer 56-tick timer expires. The `0x13b3a` composite pose
validates both facing records and exports its 13 tile codes and signed
per-tile coordinates. Source origin `0x0169` resolves through the shared CPS
coordinate-template pointer table at `0x3b9b2`, applies the signed
origin-table displacement, and reaches the 13 signed coordinate pairs at
`0x3e9fe`; the catalog checks the pointer table, displacement, and resolved
coordinates against the offline source image when generating native data.
Descriptor `0x0011`/`0x0031` marks independent 16-by-16 tiles and horizontal
flipping. The native renderer draws all 13 tiles and mirrors each tile
coordinate for the opposite facing. Cue `0x34` still needs native sequenced
audio.
The main CPU's `0x1f30` selector and `0x1f4c` advance routine only install and
step the pointer/timer fields; a scan of the rebuilt reference program finds
their corresponding duplicate cursor at `0x4972`/`0x49b4`, but no frame-list
decoder at those sites. The composite still requires tracing the shared sprite
submission path that consumes those object fields. Other frame-pointer reads
at `0x70e0` and `0x7798` use record word 3 to select collision-bound tables
(`0x3b0d2` and `0x3b1aa`); they do not consume the tile-code list.
The queue-class-10 selector-0 handler at `0x2359c` dispatches further on byte
`+33`; its initial state installs vector `0xed524` and animation table
`0x23856`, then jumps to `0x2162`. The catalog validates this handler entry and
its initialization, providing the native actor's first source-backed state
data. Willow's state-6 substate-4 expiry at `0x129fc` calls spawn helper
`0x12dfa` when player byte `+33` is not 6. The Stage 0 player object starts
with byte `+33` clear, so this is a verified native gameplay entry point: it
queues sound command `0x34`, allocates the class-10 selector-0 actor at Willow's
position plus the facing vector from `0x12e46`, and passes the selected facing
to its animation table. The opening pose uses tile `0x1362`; selector-0 state 2
holds it for 64 updates and calls `0x3d90` on every fourth global frame.
Contact or timeout selects the same state-4 terminal route: animation table
`0x23b06` displays `0x13ae`, `0x13af`, and `0x13ef` for four ticks each, then
state 6 reaches the `0x2b6a` cleanup path. The native runtime now mirrors this
stationary timing, solid-probe cadence, terminal animation, and cleanup across
up to 20 modeled selector-0 records, with the source LIFO allocation and
cleanup order. Other class-10 behavior selectors are not integrated into this
pool model. Every active modeled actor updates each frame; up to two visible
effects are drawn through Genesis sprite slots 78 and 79. Its
periodic terrain check now follows source `0x3d90`'s profile-zero point and
`0x44ea` contact predicate, including bit-3 shape contact and bit-0/bit-1
directional fallbacks without movement correction. The renderer now culls the
effect origin against the camera-relative `0x2244` window, independent of
Willow's screen anchor. The cue `0x34` still needs
the native sequence player.
The primary child allocator `0x2b04` draws from a 20-record, 64-byte pool
initialized at `0x26f2` with queue class 8; its first allocation after reset
takes record 19, followed by records 18, 17, and 16. Its class-8 entry at
`0xec84` initializes the 64-tick horizontal mover; state 2 uses one of the
source `0xed0c` vectors and state 6 returns the record through `0x2b20`. The
native runtime now follows this lifetime, movement, periodic camera cull, and
LIFO allocation/cleanup for all 20 records. Separate tile caches and the
32-sprite reservation cover the first four visible children. The class-8
animation streams at `0xf040` and `0xf074` now drive each actor's exact four
frames, three-tick holds, dimensions, flip, and origin. The terrain/collision
helper `0x3744` is modeled with directional point correction and state-4 impact
animation. Genesis palette and color matching still needs visual review.

The source conditionally takes a second object from a separate free list at
`0x29d0`, writes active type 1, behavior 1, and copies the player's movement
selector from byte `+15`, but writes no coordinates at `0xcc28`. Reset path
`0x2648` initializes this 20-entry, 64-byte pool at `0x293e` with queue class
2. The class-2 dispatcher at `0xfb48` sends behavior 1 to `0xfe3e`; this is
distinct from the class-4 actor handler at `0x115ee`. Behavior 1 initializes
active type 2, state 2, and an eight-tick timer, and selects one of two
four-record animation streams at `0xfea8`. The first three frames hold for
four ticks and the final frame is a long hold. Each state-2 update advances
the animation, decrements the timer, sets X to the shared target X plus 16 or
minus 16 according to facing, sets Y to target Y plus 8, and invokes
visibility. After the timer expires, the next state-4 update returns the
record through `0x29ec` to the class-2 LIFO free list.

The native charge-release child now follows that class-2 behavior: it uses the
source four-frame animation and horizontal flip, target-relative coordinates,
eight-tick lifetime, visibility update, and pool cleanup. The animation
catalog validates the dispatcher, state handlers, free routine, and both
source streams. This corrects the earlier model that incorrectly gave this
record the 72-tick `0x115ee` movement lifecycle. The separate actor allocated
at `0xa28a` uses class-12 handler `0x3257e`; the source `0x26f2e` counter
writer belongs to a queue-class-18 parent, and its relation to charge release
is not established. That parent still does not justify connecting the two
lifecycles.
The writer is a queue-class-18 actor processed by the eight-record manager at
`0x2690`/`0x26dae`. A type-0 creator at `0x14a20` allocates one of these actors
at world X 3600 and player world Y +56 from a timed stage-script state. Its
reachability during normal Stage 0 play has not been proven, so it is not
connected to any Stage 0 actor cleanup. The offline object
catalog validates the class-18 pool, dispatcher, writer context, type-0
creator, and later-stage behavior-index-7 route. The stage-counter-3 branch
creates behavior index 7, whose state-6 handler reaches the creator. This
confirms that later-stage path does not justify firing Stage 0 cleanup. The
catalog also validates both allocations, both pool setups, the primary
child's startup, walk, wait, proximity, contact, and voice paths, the class-2
behavior-1 release child, and the separate class-4 actor's mode-0 lifecycle.
The later-stage counter writer remains a separate, unconnected route.
The burst handler `0xce32` applies the full signed 8.8 X vector before calling
`0x3814` once at the resulting position. That helper checks its two leading
points with facing property bits and shape classes; its property correction is
written to the shared probe coordinates, not applied to the actor's `+6` X.
The routine indexes two 64-byte point tables with object byte `+71`; all four
profile entries in each table contain the same facing-specific point pairs.
Native burst movement now applies the complete vector first and performs one
two-point collision probe at the destination, matching the source update order.
Enemy damage and hit outcomes remain unported.
The
source queues sound command `0x31` when the charge reaches 16. The offline
audio-CPU disassembly shows commands arriving through shared sound memory and
being passed to its sequencer; `0x31` is not an OKI sample-table index. The
sequencer uses two modulo tables: the fixed table at `0x0e6d` selects cue 17,
then bank 1's table at CPU address `0x8000` resolves it to sequence address
`0x8f6b` (ROM file offset `0xcf6b`). The command-to-sequence address is now
recorded for all low-bit commands in `build/willow_audio_commands.json`, along
with each cue's eight raw track addresses, ROM prefixes, and first event's
parser branch. For command `0x31`, the nonempty entries point to `0x2f00`,
`0x0018`, `0x0600`, `0x030e`, `0x008a`, and `0x0f00`. Its first track starts
with control byte `0x11`, whose dispatch word at `0x0974` is `0x3e0b`; this word
falls beyond the visible 16-entry control-handler table and overlaps following
code, so its meaning remains unresolved. The `0xff7f` entry is also unresolved.
The catalog now validates the main-CPU control-flow contexts for the charge
threshold write at `0xc672` and the saturated-charge repeat at `0xc6ba`, so
these cues are no longer just raw instruction-pattern candidates.
The sequence bytecode and its YM/OKI events still need decoding
before the native port can reproduce the cue. A separate audio-CPU command path confirms that command
`0x8a` selects OKI sample `0x0a` and voice mask `0x2`: the sound CPU reduces the
command through its 42-entry table at `0x0e43`, then writes the sample and
voice/volume bytes to the OKI register at `0xf002`. That mapping is not used by
the native charge action because its source command is `0x31`. The
developer asset browser uses A/B to play/stop the selected PCM sample; those
controls are separate from the native movement prototype. Command `0x8a` is
verified in the profile-1 actor's behavior-selector-1 wait path, but the
Stage 0 state-4 child descriptors resolve only to selectors 2 and 5. Its actor
creation path is therefore still unresolved, and the native game does not
trigger this voice yet.
`tools/cps1_audio_catalog.py` exports the 112 direct-OKI commands (`0x80-0xef`),
the 16 system commands (`0xf0-0xff`), and all 128 low-bit sequence-table
lookups to `build/willow_audio_commands.json`. This follows the Z80 command
router at `0x0132`, direct-sample handler at `0x03d2`, system dispatch table at
`0x02ee`, and sequence tables at `0x0e6d` and bank 1. It records verified
source contexts for charge cues `0x31` and `0x44`, burst cue `0x2a`, jump cue
`0x2b`, the profile-1 voice `0x8a`, and direct command `0x83`. The JSON is an
offline source-mapping aid; it is not linked into the native ROM. The catalog
now validates the Z80 cue pointer loader and basic event classes: control
bytes below `0x20`, timing bytes `0x20-0x3f`, and note bytes `0x40-0xff`.
Command `0x20` sets the following-byte low-nibble countdown plus one; other
timing commands store the low-nibble delay. YM instrument/envelope setup,
note-to-register conversion, and playback timing still need decoding before
these cues or the soundtrack can be recreated faithfully. It also records raw-byte candidates for immediate
main-CPU sound-helper calls. Among them, the charge state sends `0x31` at
`0xc672` and `0x44` at `0xc6ba`, while the burst state sends cue `0x2a` at
`0xcdf0`; all three resolve to sequenced cues, not direct OKI samples. A
call at `0xcef8` is verified inside state zero of the actor-byte-`+3`
dispatcher at `0xced4`; it sends direct
command `0x83` (sample `0x03`, voice mask `0x2`). That handler sets a 40-tick
timer, advances its substate, toggles the low facing bit, and selects animation
table `0xd436`; timer expiry sets actor byte `+2` to state 6. The audio catalog
validates the dispatcher, command write, and follow-up timer path. The adjacent
controller routine at `0xcdc2` dispatches through a separate actor-byte-`+4`
table and does not call `0xced4`; it is not established as this handler's
parent. The identity of the object using `0xced4`, and its relationship to
Willow's native `0x12780` normal-entry handler, are not established, so command
`0x83` has no native gameplay trigger.
The audio asset converter also emits sample `0x03` in the 16 kHz PCM4 bank,
and
the native direct-OKI dispatcher routes command `0x83` to that asset when
called. This prepares the verified sample path without assigning it a guessed
player action; its source handler trigger remains unresolved. Sample `0x0a`
continues to use its Stage 0 verified PCM4 path.
The catalog also validates a conditional direct-OKI pair at `0xc1b6` in the
shared controller helper `0xc170`. The Stage 0 gameplay dispatcher at
`0xc13e` calls this helper on every active update. When global byte
`a5+0x0362` is positive and `a5+0x0364` changes from its mirror at
`a5+0x0389`, fixed-record byte `+32` (`a5+0x1866`) selects command `0x82` or
`0x84`. These resolve to samples `0x02` and `0x04`, both on OKI voice 2 at full
volume. The helper then sets record timer `+54` to 128 and animation timer
`+78` to 4. The three currently validated direct writers to `a5+0x0364`
(at `0x345e8`, `0x34620`, and `0x34658`) immediately copy each new value to
the `a5+0x0389` mirror, so those writes by themselves cannot satisfy the
helper's inequality. A reachable direct or indirect writer that leaves the
mirror different has not been identified; the fixed record's `+32` value is
also unresolved. Native gameplay therefore has no source-backed trigger for
these sounds yet.
The native Stage 0 jump no longer borrows descent or landing transitions from
the unlinked `0xc8f2` path. Its `0xc7ec` transition performs the first vertical
movement at `0xc7f4` and checks the Stage 0 profile-3 points from
`0x39fe`/`0x3f62` at `(-10,+24),(+10,+24)`, including source Y-fraction
correction. The `0xc820` ascent handler applies the `0x38f6` facing-side probes
at `(+12,-24),(-12,-24)` (reversed when facing left), with the
`0x3e4c` solid-shape correction. Ascent checks the profile-3 `0x403c`
signed-shape point at `(-10,+40)` or `(+10,+40)` according to facing, then the
`0x3fa2` fallback at the facing side's `(+/-8,+40)`, while Genesis Up is held,
following the source's
input bit-3 gate at `0xc57a`. The CPS1 input table maps bit 3 to joystick Up;
the same bit selects the larger `0x0580` launch velocity at `0xc7bc` (otherwise
`0x0440`). Holding Genesis Up selects the stronger launch and gates the
source ascent probe. Jump handlers apply vertical velocity directly and skip
the full `0x208c` movement-vector helper, while the shared dispatcher calls
`0x20b4` for an X-only vector step. `0xc52a` selects rows 0/1 from left/right
input during both the transition and ascent; neutral input sets zero-X rows
2/3. The native jump path follows those row selections and then uses state 8's
own source vector after its entry update.
The active alternate jump route duplicates that ascent handler at `0xdc90`.
On contact, it checks the `0x38f6` profile unless byte +36 is already set;
either hit path clears jump mode and state bytes at `0xdca4`, selects the
current direction, and queues sequenced cue `0x2b`. The alternate state-zero
handler at `0xdaec` runs on the next update. This selector-1 reset remains
cataloged separately; native Stage 0 does not apply it. That handler clears
source fields `+62/+71`, advances
substate `+4`, selects animation table `0xe194`, then applies vector movement
and collision. This selector-1 reset is cataloged separately; the native
Stage 0 player follows the selector-0 `0xc78a/0xc7bc` jump path and does not
apply `0xe194`. The Stage 0 collision exit resumes its normal walk/idle pose.
Cue `0x2b` remains unresolved for native playback.
The native ascent collision caller now passes the actor origin to the helper;
the helper itself applies the `0x3b02` primary and `0x3afa` fallback offsets,
each with one `+40` Y displacement. The collision catalog validates the
`0x3a84` primary/fallback dispatch and exports both offset tables as native
data, preventing the prior double-offset error from returning unnoticed.
The native loop now preserves left/right facing changes in the air and applies
the source's horizontal jump steering without adding its steady table-driven Y
drift. A successful upward probe at `0xc57a` enters top-level state 8 through
`0xc892` or `0xdce0`. This is separate from the 26-tick state-6 falling
transition in the indexed handler at `0xc906`: state 8 starts animation
`0x13154` and uses the slow vector rows at `0x136b8` (±1 X, −2 Y). Its
movement/contact handler loops through additional vector steps in the same
actor update while byte +31 remains clear; its 60-step movement timer changes
to a 56-tick `0x1315c` pose before the cycle repeats. The `0x12d92` check runs
every eight frames and enters state 4 when the player is inside its target
window. Source handler `0x12ae4` installs the normal `0x136b0` movement vector
and branches to `0x1283e`, which sets top-level state 4/substate 0. Native
state-8 exit now resumes target-following movement with substate 0;
it no longer enters the separate `+0x0400` ballistic recovery path. Normal
state 2 enters `0x1283e` when byte +31 is clear; a set byte +31 calls `0x1f4c`
before its vertical and timer gates. Native now follows this polarity and
tracks top-level state 4 separately, reuses ordinary movement, and gates
the state-4 timer check only after +31 contact in vertical band 4, following
handler `0x1284a`. State 4 clears substate +4 to zero when +31 is clear,
returns without animation, and calls `0x1f4c` when +31 is set; native now
follows that split. Clear-contact state-2 and state-8-exit transition ticks
preserve the active animation when the source returns before `0x1f4c`,
while a timer transition keeps the preceding state-2 animation advance. The
normal actor uses the six-frame, eight-tick `0x13154` animation in states 2
and 4; the `0xd07e` six-tick loops belong to the fixed input controller. After
a state-4 timed-mask hit, native also applies the source `0x20d2` heading gate
and clears substate only for heading 10 facing right or heading 6 facing left.
The collision catalog validates these transition instructions, both state-8
entry sites, the timed handlers,
vector bytes, and exit bounds; the native loop models the movement/contact
loop, pose cycle, and target-window exit. When the 56-tick pose ends at
`0x12b6a`, the source reselects `0x13154` through `0x1f30`, loading its first
8-tick hold; the native pose return now resets that animation timer to eight.
The animation catalog now resolves the `0x1315c` coordinate-template record
into its 11 tile codes and signed per-tile positions. The Genesis renderer
streams the two composite poses at their 16-tick and terminal holds after the
20-tick entry pose; rendered comparison and exact contact side effects remain
to be checked.
The 26-tick falling sequence at `0xc8f2/0xc906/0xc958/0xc988/0xc9da` is
validated source data, but its connection to the Stage 0 controller and Willow
actor remains unproven; native Stage 0 does not use it. For the verified
`0xc820` ascent, native collision uses the profile-3 `0x38f6` facing-side
probes at `(+12,-24),(-12,-24)` (reversed when facing left), with the
`0x3e4c` solid-shape snap before exiting the jump handler. Negative shapes
with bit 6 apply the source's corrected-Y tile reload and secondary shape
check. Nondefault collision profiles and other state side effects remain
unmodeled. The jump tiles from
`0x06c0-0x073f` stream uncompressed to a separate VRAM range. Hit detection,
damage, health, and progression remain unfinished. The audio browser
demonstrates four-channel 14 kHz XGM PCM playback. Charging sends sequenced commands
`0x31` at the 16-tick threshold and `0x44` every 16 ticks after saturation;
the latter resolves to cue `0x8dc5`, not direct OKI sample `0x04`. Neither cue
has been reproduced in the native game yet; music and other game sound events
remain unfinished. The developer PCM browser and direct OKI cues use SGDK's XGM
driver, so digitized clips can coexist with future XGM music.

The jump source also queues sequenced sound command `0x2b` at `0xc86c` when
the ascent collision path exits the jump state; it is not a direct OKI sample.
The offline sound catalog resolves it to sequence address `0x8e99` (bank 1
ROM offset `0xce99`), with nonempty track pointers at `0x002a`, `0x0011`,
`0x0300`, and `0x2aff`. The event bytecode and YM/OKI effects are not decoded
enough to reproduce this cue. The catalog now validates its instruction
boundary and collision-exit branch against the source bytes before marking
the call as verified. Native jump collision currently omits this sound.

The unusual low-address pointers do not by themselves make those streams
invalid: Z80 routine `0x01fa` copies all eight pointers, and scheduler `0x0453`
skips a track only when its pointer is zero. For cue `0x2b`, track 2 at
`0x002a` begins with bytes `5e 23 56 23 c9`, which the event parser reads as
note/timing/control events even though the same bytes are executable code in
the fixed sound ROM. Tracks 1 and 4 point to unmapped addresses `0xff0a` and
`0xff00`; under the catalogued MAME map their first read is zero and enters
control event 0 at `0x0972`. The handler consumes an operand, forms `HL` from
`(0x80 + operand) << 8`, applies three `SRL H` operations and one `RR L`, and
stores the result in global sound-RAM note-table pointer `0xd015` or `0xd017`
according to Z80 RAM selector `0xd01a`. This selects note-table state, not a
track-stream destination: note setup at `0x08a4` reads the selected pointer
and uses it as the base for note lookup. The catalog now validates both byte
sequences. Note-table contents, resulting key conversion, and YM register
effects remain open. The audio JSON includes bounded linear note/timing
prefixes for mapped tracks and stops at the first control event rather than
assuming control operands are inline.
For cue `0x2b` tracks `0xff0a` and `0xff00`, MAME's unmapped-read default
supplies zero for both the event byte and event-0 operand. The validated
handler therefore stores note-table base `0x1000` in the selected global
pointer. This is a software-map derivation; physical open-bus behavior and the
musical meaning of the table data still need hardware/source verification.
This evidence does not justify dropping the valid fixed-ROM tracks or
substituting direct OKI samples.

The player knockback handler at `0xc72e` is now traced as an implementation
lead: while collision byte `+36` is clear, it applies the signed horizontal
velocity from `+58` to the player's 16.16 X position and clamps the velocity
to `0x0700`. At `+58 >= 0x0180` it switches to state `+3 = 2`, substate
`+4 = 4`, sets field `+72` to 2, clears `+56` and `+71`, and resumes through
`0x3b0a`. The source has six direct player-state branches to this handler at
`0xc3d8`, `0xc9f6`, `0xcdde`, `0xdae2`, `0xddbe`, and `0xe046`; each follows
`JSR 0x38f6`. The object catalog now validates all six call contexts. These
are terrain-response movement paths: `0x38f6` selects the player's collision
profile, probes the Scroll 2 properties through `0x3e28`/`0x3e4c`, combines
their contact mask, and writes it to player `+36` before `0xc72e` consumes it.
The catalog validates these probe and flag-write instructions. They do not
show that the Stage 0 actor sets the contact byte or damages Willow. The
generic enemy attack scan at
`0x10c9c` still changes enemy state and animation without calling this player
handler, so the attack pose still does not prove a hit. Its entry gate exits
when `a5+0x188e` is set, when the stage counter is 3, or when the 16-bit
expression `actorY - targetY + 30` is below 60 under the source's unsigned
comparison. This is the source's near-target band (with 16-bit wraparound at
the coordinate limits). Outside that band, it performs direction-specific
`0x3c40` terrain probes: the `actorY <= targetY` branch checks four points at
Y offsets +39, +55, +71, and +87, and a successful probe enters state 2 with a
16-tick timer and animation `0x113fa`; the `actorY > targetY` branch first
checks an extra point at Y-32 for collision mode 4 and exits if that point is
not solid, then checks four points at Y-80, Y-96, Y-112, and Y-128. A hit in
that scan enters state 6 with the same timer and animation `0x11416`. Neither branch
writes Willow's health or state. This pins the
modeled attack transition to a terrain-gated enemy animation, without
inventing player damage. I also traced a
separate possible contact-flag producer: `0x6e44` iterates actor queues at
`a5+0x1805/0x1806`, dispatches candidates by byte `+32`, and the overlap branch
at `0x6eb8` can set the current record's `+36` flag after repositioning it.
Caller `0x2d1aa` then tests that flag. The object catalog validates these byte
paths and the candidate type map at `0x6e96`: behavior types 0, 1, and 2 have
callbacks, while type 3 maps to `0xff` and is rejected as a candidate. That
filter does not reject Willow when she is the current record, but the source
caller is in a class-14 actor pool: initializer `0x28de` creates 60 records
of 64 bytes at `a5+0x5bc6` and sets byte `+30` to 14, and scheduler `0x2cf90`
dispatches those records through byte `+32`. This scan is therefore an actor
interaction path, not evidence of Willow receiving damage. The class-8 peer
scan at `0x37b5e` also does not establish damage: it walks the 20-record pool
at `a5+0x42c6`, checks actor rectangles, and dispatches candidate byte `+32`
through the relative table at `0x37bd0`. Its validated callbacks change state
byte `+0` and collision counter `+42`; they do not write Willow's `+36` contact
flag or health. The catalog validates the scan body, callback table, and
callback bodies. The Stage 0
type-2 actor is allocated from the queue-12 pool at `0x2756`; its pool
initializer sets byte `+30` to 12, and allocator `0x2b9c` preserves it. Its
visibility helper `0x2244` therefore dispatches to `0x242e`; byte `+14=2`
routes that callback to list `a5+0x1838` (count `a5+0x180f`). The contact
scanner reads only `a5+0x1805` and `a5+0x1806`, so this actor's verified
visibility path does not insert it into either scanned list. Willow's own
normal actor handler at `0x1270c` sets `+14=2`; its class-12 callback at
`0x242e` routes that value to `0x2452`, which inserts her into `a5+0x1838`
(count `a5+0x180f`). The normal handler reaches visibility helper `0x2244`
at `0x1276a`. The separate pairwise scan at `0x3b25c` reads `a5+0x181e` and
`a5+0x1826`; it also does not scan Willow's verified queue. These known
overlap scanners therefore do not establish an enemy-to-Willow hit. The
separate selector-4 handler at `0x13bd2` is now connected to its creator:
the main-pool loop at `0x00cc90` allocates active selector-4 records at the
current actor's X and Y (or Y-8 when byte `+62` is set), with child byte
`+15` counting from 7 down to 0. In handler state 2, source instruction
`0x13c16` writes `+14=2`; the later state dispatcher reaches visibility helper
`0x2244`. The object catalog validates both the allocator loop and selector
write. This establishes a render-queue route for these actors, but not their
owner's Stage 0 reachability or a damage connection to Willow. The
`a5+0x1838` list is drained by `0x3b7a0`, which passes each record to `0x3b880`
for animation and render-list processing; the object catalog byte-validates
this consumer. A disassembly cross-reference of the direct `a5+0x1838` and
`a5+0x180f` field accesses finds only the queue insertion at `0x2452`, pool
initialization at `0x281e`, and render-list drain at `0x3b7a0`; the adjacent
instructions update the queue head and count at those same sites. Those
accesses cover insertion, reset, and rendering, with no additional direct
consumer among the decoded main-CPU instructions. This narrows the known Stage
0 route without ruling out indirect or differently indexed damage paths. The
additional scanner at `0x743a` walks a separate candidate list at
`a5+0x1805/0x1824`; its byte map admits behavior types 2 and 3, and their
shared response at `0x748e` can set the current actor's `+36`. The seven direct
callers now validated in the object catalog use that flag for actor state,
animation, terrain, or child-allocation behavior. They do not establish the
current actor as Willow or insert Willow's `a5+0x1838` record into the scanned
candidate list. Other Stage 0 enemy/player damage routes remain unresolved. A second scan at
`0x39ade` uses the fixed record at
`a5+0x1846` as its current object and walks the same two lists through a
separate candidate-type table. Its type-0 overlap response at `0x39bba`
has two horizontal branches: one repositions current Y to candidate Y + 22,
clears current `+12` and `+58`, and sets current `+36=1` and candidate
`+36=2`; the other sets candidate `+36=1` only. A miss clears candidate
`+36`.
The byte tables and this response are now validated by the object catalog.
The `a5+0x1846` record is the active Stage 0 fixed input controller and shared
target, separate from Willow's actor; it is not the player hurt record. The
state-2 writer at `0x3a66c` is shared: it is
reached from the player terrain probe at `0x00c320` and an object-overlap
handler at `0x029084`. That makes the record's state transition
insufficient evidence of a player hurt event; the catalog validates both
caller contexts and records the ambiguity.

The `0x39ab8` path also calls `0x3a6aa` while the fixed record is in state 1.
That routine scans candidates in lists `a5+0x181e/0x1820` and
`a5+0x1802/0x1803`, filters active records by byte `+32`, and tests their
frame-derived collision bounds against the fixed record. Matching callbacks
can reach `0x3a66c`: when `a5+0x0364` is nonzero, it decrements that byte and
one of `a5+0x035c/+0x035a/+0x035b`; otherwise it decrements `a5+0x0362`. A
pending timer at `a5+0x035d` takes a separate 128-tick response. This is a
source-backed controller-overlap path and can explain how `a5+0x0364` changes
without immediately updating the `a5+0x0389` audio mirror. Its candidate lists
have not yet been tied to the native Stage 0 enemy records, and these counters
are not verified as player health, so native enemy damage remains unresolved.
The collision catalog now extracts the 175 actor-frame rectangles from
`0x3ac4a` and the 19 fixed-controller frame rectangles from `0x3b1c2` into
`willow_collision.json` and the generated header. It validates the scan,
frame-index selection, and overlap callback instructions. These tables are
ready for native use; the class-4/player overlap loop and its frame selection
are not yet implemented.

The object catalog separately validates the queue-class-6 pool used by
`0x6e44`'s candidate lists: 48 records of 64 bytes, free-list count at `a5+0x1804`, and head at
`a5+0x1822`. Its visibility callback can append records to the two scanned
lists. Six allocation contexts are recorded with their written or inherited
positions, including fixed-position actors, parent-attached actors, and a
camera-relative actor. The fixed pair at world `(2048, 80)` and `(2192, 80)`
sits in behavior-7 handler `0x1432c`; the stage-counter-3 setup at `0xa198`
creates that behavior. The other four allocation owners remain unresolved.
None is connected to normal Stage 0 startup, so the native port does not
create them as unverified contact targets. See `class6_contact_pool` in
`build/willow_objects.json` for the source-byte checks.
The class-6 dispatch table further connects selector 20 at `0x2f414` to
handler `0x33a56`. Its timer path creates main-pool behavior-19 actors at
`0x33ad4`, selecting their byte `+33` from `0x33b18`; selector 0 then causes
main-pool handler `0x1a7f2` to create class-6 behavior-1 candidates at
`(2336, 256)`. The originating class-6 behavior-20 actor still has no traced
normal Stage 0 creator, so this chain remains disabled in native gameplay.
There is also a separate 48-record, 64-byte actor pool at `a5+0x0502`, reset
by `0x29a4` and stepped by `0x3809c`. Its type-3 handler at `0x39814` can
create queue-class-6 actors at `0x398b4`, copying the parent's byte `+16` into
the candidate's behavior selector. The route that creates a type-3 parent
with selector 20 during normal Stage 0 remains unresolved; this pool must not
be confused with the queue-class-6 candidate pool itself.
The record is initialized on the normal Stage 0 setup path: `0xa0e0` calls
`0x2f08`, which sets its byte `+0` to 1 after a stage-counter dispatch. Its
coordinate words `+6/+10` alias `a5+0x184c/+0x1850`, also used by source
actors as global target coordinates. The catalog now byte-validates this
initializer and caller. This confirms the record is active in Stage 0, but
does not identify it with Willow's moving player record.

MAME's `WL24B` mapper selects CPS graphics address windows for sprites,
Scroll 3, Scroll 1, and bank 1 Scroll 2. The native asset exporter writes the
mapped layer pixels as Genesis tile streams. Stage 0 Scroll 2/3 tilemaps and
cell-boundary scrolling are now reconstructed in the native renderer; Scroll 1
screens are cataloged by purpose, but the ordinary gameplay foreground/HUD
call path is still unverified. The player uses the uncompressed sprite stream
and uploads active frames from cartridge ROM in VBlank DMA batches.

## Build

Requirements are SGDK, Java for SGDK resource conversion, and the `m68k-elf`
toolchain. Set `SGDK_ROOT` to a compatible SGDK checkout. The release target
uses SGDK's no-LTO makefile because the provided SGDK library was built with
GCC 13 LTO data and cannot link with newer cross-compilers. On this machine,
`.tools/sgdk-build` is an isolated SGDK copy whose library was rebuilt for the
installed compiler; use it with:

```sh
export SGDK_ROOT=.tools/sgdk-build
make assets
make release
```

`make assets` writes the complete decoded stream to
`build/willow_genesis_tiles.bin`, offline Scroll 1/2/3 tile streams, the
animation- and stage-referenced uncompressed packs, generated animation and
stage headers, the palette header, and OKI clips in `build/oki_wav/`.
`make release` creates `out/rom.bin`; the current finalized image is 8,388,608
bytes. It contains
the uncompressed packed animation sprites, stage-referenced Scroll 2 and
Scroll 3 graphics and map chunks, and 40 source OKI clips converted to
14,000 Hz 8-bit XGM PCM, plus the source-attenuated variant for sample `0x19`
used by commands `0x99`, `0xc3`, and `0xed`.
The 40 distinct valid samples also occupy one 16 kHz signed 8-bit PCM4 bank;
sample `0x19` uses PCM4's mapped source volume. The source command's voice mask
and attenuation select the matching asset. The Stage 0 event for sample `0x0a` and
the unresolved `0x03` object handler retain their documented runtime status;
generating assets does not establish gameplay triggers for the other cues.
SGDK's PCM4 driver reads its samples from a stable ROM address. The native
playback path maps the packed bank into windows 4 and 5 before playback; the
bank begins at 2 MiB, fills adjacent 512 KiB banks, and leaves subsequent
resources beyond the reserved window.
The ROM header identifies SGDK's official Sega mapper and advertises its
4 MiB CPU address window (`0x000000`–`0x3fffff`). Data beyond that window is
available through switchable 512 KiB banks; the runtime accesses far resources
through `SYS_getFarData`. The image is padded to 128 KiB and currently fits
within the mapper's 32 MiB limit. The project finalizer writes the mapped
window end address and recomputes the Sega checksum without invoking SGDK's
Java padding utility. The release audit checks the mapper header, checksum,
banked data presence, image alignment, and 32 MiB size limit. It also runs
`tools/native_rom_audit.py`, which rejects the known arcade CPU program-ROM
images from the finalized native ROM. This checks those exact source images;
it is not a general proof that all derived code is native.

`make reference-maincpu` reconstructs a 1 MiB copy of the arcade 68000 address
region under `build/` for offline disassembly. That target is deliberately
absent from `release` prerequisites and from SGDK resource declarations; no
arcade CPU program is linked or executed by the Genesis ROM.

`make layer-map-catalog` decodes the fixed-size Scroll 2 and Scroll 3 chunks
from the offline ROM image into `build/willow_layer_maps.json`. Disassembly
shows the map viewer copying 512 words (256 code/attribute cell pairs) from
`0x80000 + index*0x400` to Scroll 2 RAM and 128 words (64 pairs) from
`0xc0000 + index*0x100` to Scroll 3 RAM. Scroll 3 adds `0x0a00` to each code.
Both CPS-1 layer maps scan column first, with the row as the low-order cell
address; the native gameplay renderer, collision probes, and offline previews
use this same layout.
The offline preview reads each code/attribute pair, applies Scroll 2's graphics
bank mapping, tile flips, and the source CPS palette blocks, and renders
out-of-range Scroll 3 codes as transparent. Select a source palette with
`--palette-index` (Scroll 2: 0..10; Scroll 3: 0..7); the default is zero.
Scroll 3 applies the game's per-stage palette-half selection and retains the
default palette half where the stage does not replace it. For example,
`python3 tools/cps1_layer_map_preview.py scroll2 10 --output
build/scroll2_10.ppm` previews a terrain chunk with source colors. This restores
the per-tile palette group colors, but not layer priority, transparency between
layers, or the selected gameplay palette state. These are confirmed map-viewer
data paths. The catalog remains offline reference material and is not linked
into the release image.

The viewer routines are separate from gameplay. The older research path
at `0x43984..0x43b18` was initially assumed to select one of eight 256-byte chunk-selector grids through
the pointer table at `0x2eb24`; the selector mode table at `0x2eb44` is zero for
all eight. Lookup routine `0x436c2` maps world chunk coordinates to a 16x16
selector grid. Each byte selects both a Scroll 2 map chunk from `0x80000` and a
Scroll 3 map chunk from `0xc0000`. `make stage-catalog` extracts these grids to
`build/willow_stage_maps.json` and a C header for native streaming. The selector
tables establish which map chunks belong to gameplay stages. Scroll 2 and
Scroll 3 palette source tables and stage-dependent Scroll 3 palette halves are
also cataloged. The initializer at `0x43984-0x439a0` indexes the selector
pointer table directly with the stage field at `a5+0x0344`; grids 0–5 therefore
correspond directly to those stage values. The exact instruction bytes at the
transition gate `0xa902-0xa922` and normal transition `0xa93e-0xa974` are now
checked by the catalog. The gate requires `a5+0x02a6` clear, the word timer at
`a5+0x000a` to reach zero, and the byte at `a5-0x8e85` to underflow below zero.
The controller dispatch table at `0xa610` is indexed by the byte-offset state
at `a5+0x0008`; its state-7, state-8, and state-9 entries target `0xa7b8`,
`0xa8b4`, and `0xa902`. State 6 at `0xa79e` waits for `a5+0x7891` to clear,
then advances the controller to state 7. State 7 performs stage-dependent
setup and advances to state 8. Its continuation at `0xa832` loads the stage's
starting message index from the six-byte table at `0xa8ae`
(`[0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0]`) into countdown byte `a5-0x8e85`. State 8 at `0xa8b4`
The preceding entry at `0xa63e` calls `0x2884` to reset the 20-record actor
pool, then tests bit 1 of shared byte `a5+0x03c3`. When clear, it sets timer
`a5+0x7892` to one, loads a stage-indexed input-script pointer from `0xa626`
into `a5+0x7894`, and advances the controller state. When set, it changes
state to 4. The timer handler at `0x2020` reads four-byte records, copies the
input-mask byte at record `+1` into `a5+0x006a`, loads the frame duration from
`+2`, and advances the pointer. The caller at `0xd03a` derives the new input
edge from current and previous masks and writes it to `a5-0x8e92`. This is a
timed input playback path; it does not explain ordinary player input or stage
completion. Ten immediate stores to `a5+0x03c3` are validated: two store 1
and eight store 2, from several actor state and timer routines. Its active
writer on the normal Stage 0 path remains untraced.

advances to state 9, sets the word timer to 60, and uses the current countdown
value to select a message ID from the stage record at `0xa8ea`. State 9 waits
60 ticks, decrements that same index, and if it remains nonnegative clears
text-map rows through `0x7d70` and loops back to state 8. A negative result
advances the stage. Therefore each stage displays the selected record prefix
in reverse index order: stage records `[27]`, `[2e, 2d]`, `[41, 40, 2f]`,
`[45, 44]`, `[46]`, `[48]` display as `[27]`, `[2d, 2e]`, `[2f, 40, 41]`,
`[44, 45]`, `[46]`, `[48]`, with a 60-tick wait for each message. State 8
clears D1, loads the selected message ID into its low byte, then launches an asynchronous
`0x0c00` task at slot `0xc0`. Trap `0x15d0` stores the whole D1 word at task
field `+0x10`. The handler at `0x78f0` reads the high byte at `+0x10` as a
handler type; zero selects the generic text parser at `0x7912`, while
the low byte at `+0x11` carries the message ID. The scheduler's selected
slot pointer at `a5-0x7dfc` (`0x1506`) is the same record loaded into A6,
confirming both bytes are read from this task. The parser resolves the message
record at `0x70000 + message_id * 0xa8`, starts the string eight bytes into that
record, treats `&` as a line break and `/` as its terminator, then writes
character tile codes beginning at `0x7000`. These are narrative message IDs,
not enemy spawn IDs. `make stage-catalog` now extracts and validates the
normal-route messages into `build/willow_stage_maps.json`; native intermission
presentation and its connection to gameplay progression remain to be
implemented. State 4 at `0xa756`
calls `0xabd8` and advances to state 5 only when byte `a5-0x717c` is clear;
that handoff starts a 120-tick timer consumed by state 5. Its nonzero branch
queues sound `0x30` and diverts through `0xaa9a`/`0xab5e`. The per-stage event
gate now records how that retry branch ends: state 3 initializes the low two
bits of `a5-0x8e84` to `3`; `0xaa9a` clears bit 0 when the unsigned value at
`a5-0x8e74` reaches `a5+0x03c6`, and `0xab5e` clears bit 1 when
`a5-0x8e80` reaches `a5-0x8e7c`. State 4 proceeds only after both bits clear.
The stage catalog checks these five instruction sites and exports the
comparisons. State 3 also initializes the backing values at `0xa994` and
`0xa9ea`: the first clears `a5-0x8e70`/`a5-0x8e74` and seeds
`a5-0x8e73` from the stage timer; the second clears `a5-0x8e78`/`a5-0x8e80`
and seeds `a5-0x8e7b` from stage-dependent work fields. The catalog now
validates both initializer blocks. The corresponding controller tick routines
at `0xaa9a`/`0xab5e` increment `a5-0x8e74`/`a5-0x8e80` in packed BCD and clear
flag bits 0/1 when those counters reach `a5+0x03c6`/`a5-0x8e7c`. Their
backing stage fields are partly resolved: `a5+0x0362` and `+0x0363` start at
5 as current/maximum sequence indices, and actor path `0x37e00` advances the
current index by one or two according to actor byte `+33`, clamps it to the
maximum, mirrors it to `+0x0365`, and refreshes the Scroll 1 display.
The update is reached through a separate dispatcher at `0x37dd0`, where
object byte `+2 == 4` selects handler `0x37e00`.
`a5+0x0364` contributes to the second counter's generated threshold, but its
complete role and exact connection to native stage events remain unresolved.
These are sequence/timing gates, not verified enemy-clear conditions, so the
native port does not use them as a stage-completion trigger.
The sequence actor's runtime pool is now traced further: dispatcher `0x36c76`
walks 20 active 64-byte records at `a5+0x6ac6`, dispatching on byte `+32`;
selector 6 reaches `0x37dd0`. The catalog also validates two ways records can
enter selector 6: an active record changes its own selector at `0x393e8` when
the frame cadence and camera-distance checks pass, and a parent handler at
`0x24560` allocates an active child with selector 6. Neither route is yet tied
to the normal Stage 0 event creation path, so this evidence does not justify
simulating sequence changes in the native game.
The active HUD timer is now separately traced: Stage 0 selects mode row 6 at
`0x8d88`, whose stage record at `0x3078` contains BCD time `0x0100` (`01:00`).
The initializer at `0x2e9c` loads that value into `a5+0x03c6` and clears the
frame subcounter at `a5+0x03c8`. Stage setup at `0x8da8` then starts a 900-tick
controller phase. Its handler at `0x8de4` decrements that phase, skips the
remaining updates when `a5+0x03c2` is nonzero, otherwise advances global frame
byte `a5+0x0019`, updates the player, and calls the timer gate at `0x4ea2`.
The four native timer digit cells now come from this source layout: writer
`0x4f18` targets Scroll 1 addresses `0x91140c` and `0x91158c`, and helper
`0x5720` advances each second digit by `0x80` bytes. The 64×64 CPS Scroll 1
mapper resolves those starts to columns 40 and 43, row 3. Startup scroll
registers apply X=-64 and Y=0, placing the timer digits at Genesis tile cells
`(32,3)`, `(33,3)`, `(35,3)`, and `(36,3)`. The stage catalog derives those
coordinates into `willow_stage_maps.h`; the runtime uses them for both drawing
and clearing the timer.
On phase exit, validated handler bytes at `0x8e14` queue system command
`0xf4`, copy two stage work-area values into actor fields `+0x18` and
`+0x0284`, clear `a5+0x1846`, advance the controller substate, and dispatch
an asynchronous text task. The temporary `D1=0x0600` is overwritten by a
message ID from the six-byte table at `0x8e50`; the initial stage counter
selects message `0x40` (`YOU CANNOT HAND ELORA OVER TO BAVMORDA. HURRY AND SAVE
HER.`), using style word `0x1422`. The native loop now starts its 900-frame
countdown with the stage controller, concurrently with the local 70-tick
opening sequence, then draws message `0x40` at Scroll 1
cell `(18,7)` with source palette group 4 while preserving the timer digits.
The native countdown now decrements before updating the Stage 0 game clock;
the clock advances only while the 900-tick phase remains active and freezes
on its expiry tick, matching the `0x8de4` branch order before call `0x4ea2`.
The story catalog now byte-validates the `0x8da8` state-4 setup and `0x8de4`
tick path, extracts the 900-tick duration from the source immediate, and checks
that expiry exits before incrementing global frame `a5+0x19` or calling the
game timer. It also extracts the 180-tick follow-up wait and the 10, 30, and
128-tick post-phase waits from their validated controller instructions. This
ties all generated native story delays to their source instructions; the
opening 70-tick sequence is derived from its 7- and 63-tick setup states, and
the following 29-tick controller wait is read from the opening task setup.
The native player-controller path now stops on phase-message entry, matching
the controller's early return before the player update. Willow remains visible
under the story message, while independent actor-dispatch updates continue.
Player-controlled movement, jump/action/recovery state, walk animation, and
range-pose timers remain frozen through the source text and transition states;
the native loop now resumes them at the controller handoff after message
`0x3f`. The shared source frame byte also stops advancing at expiry;
handler `0x8de4` branches to `0x8e14` before incrementing `a5+0x19`.
The source story extractor now also validates the following state: at
`0x8e5c` it starts a 180-tick wait and launches the next message task; Stage 0
selects message `0x41` with style `0x1423`. Its destination pointer `0x910728`
maps through `tilemap0_scan` to Scroll 1 cell `(14,10)`, so the native Window
draws it at `(9,10)` after the first message task would complete. Its exact
text and destination are emitted in `build/willow_story.h`; the native loop
holds the story display for the source 180-tick interval. The controller
wait completion at `0x8ea6` queues sound command `0x08fb`, calls `0x785e`,
increments the controller substate at `a5+0x0004`, clears `a5+0x0008`, and
returns through `0x16b4`. The source extractor validates these completion
bytes. Sound command `0xfb` reaches the Z80 handler at `0x03c1`, which loads
the duration from latch `0xf00a` (8 for this `0x08fb` call) and starts an
eight-step increase to the global mix value; the following `0xf4` resets the
sequencer. The native wait sends the sequencer stop at expiry, reproducing the
terminal silence; the short mix ramp is not separately modeled. The audio
catalog validates the handler bytes and records this effect. Its `0xf4`
handler at `0x035f` now has a byte-validated trace through the YM register
writer at `0x0117`: it clears sequencer state and does not issue an OKI stop
write. The native story transition now calls `XGM_pausePlay()` to stop audible
sequencing while preserving active XGM PCM voice channels. SGDK's pause command
clears the XGM music playing flag, loads the YM-off state, and continues into
the PCM command handler; `XGM_stopPlay()` instead runs the full stop sequence
and stops PCM channels too. This preserves active voice playback across the
source reset. The XGM stream remains paused, and source-accurate sequencer
state reconstruction is still unimplemented. The controller
dispatcher at `0x8ec4` then indexes the table at
`0x8ed0` with `a5+0x0008`; selector zero resolves to `0x8ede`. That handler
