camera mode remain unresolved.
The animation catalog validates the active camera update call path and its
Stage 0 helper branches. Those validated instructions do not write camera
target object fields `+106/+108`; this narrows the search but does not rule out
computed or aliased writes outside the scanned path. The catalog also validates
the target setup, published field, tracker, and trailing-bound helper. The
state transition to source state
6 and next-update cleanup are modeled. The verified
`0x2244` callback accepts
actor origins at `x=-32..416` and `y=0..272` relative to the camera; the native
draw window now uses those same bounds.
The renderer uses up to 30 Genesis sprite entries for this actor and shifts
the first regular enemy into the following entries. A 64-entry enemy assembly
pose is withheld during that overlap because the two actors exceed the Genesis
sprite limit; later child and effect layers also remain incomplete. Sequenced cues and the soundtrack still need native playback.

The native initial high score now comes from a generated header: the object
catalog validates source bytes `00 05 50 00` at `0x183c` as packed BCD and
exports the decoded value `55000` for the release build. The source award
handler `0x6274` is the only established caller of the current-score writer at
`0x62a0` and the high-score writer at `0x62ca`; it adds points from a queued
work event. The native HUD now displays its initial zero score and validated
55,000 high score at the traced Scroll 1 positions when the player becomes
active. Score-award updates remain unimplemented: the verified +100 event is
emitted by a class-4 actor whose Stage 0 spawn path has not been established.
A separate main-controller routine at `0xb566` is entry 8 (state 16) in the
indexed state table at `0xb12a`; the preceding entry is state 14 at `0xb4b2`,
which enters state 16 after its setup and 31-tick wait. The state-12 timer
handler at `0xb48e` advances to state 14 when its timer expires. The object
catalog now byte-validates the dispatcher, full indexed state table, and these
state-12/state-14 transitions. The ROM text immediately before this dispatch
contains “PRESENTED BY,” but the path from reset or normal Stage 0 play into
state 12 has not been established. State 16 allocates class-4
selector `0x26` at `0xb588`, then conditionally allocates two selector-1
records at `0xb5a4` and `0xb5d6`. The first allocation writes Y=256 but does
not write X before helper `0x2c86`, which only checks for a free class-4
record; X and the remaining fields are therefore inherited or unresolved.
Selector `0x26` is outside the verified 35-entry object handler table. These
actors' identities and gameplay connection remain unresolved, so they are not
used as Stage 0 enemies.

The object catalog now also validates the adjacent script at `0xa25c`: when
its existing timer expires it launches message `0x2e` (“IF YOU WANT TO KNOW
ABOUT ELORA, GO SEE THE WITCH FIN RAZIEL.”), starts a 29-tick controller
timer, and allocates the type-2 actor at `(218,136)` and Willow at `(160,80)`
in that same update. This sequence is
byte- and text-verified. It is reached on the normal stage-counter-zero path:
the dispatcher at `0x9f90` routes state 3 to `0xa0d0`, whose zero-counter
branch enters `0xa114`; that initializes position and timer 7, then state 4
at `0xa234` waits seven ticks and enters state 5 at `0xa25c`, which waits 63
ticks before queuing the message. The native runtime starts the player and
actor after the same 70-tick state-4/state-5 delay and blocks player input
during that wait. At the delay's end it renders message `0x2e` through the
Genesis Window plane for the source controller's 29-tick timer interval. The
message task itself is asynchronous: its state-0 handler enters the generic
text parser at `0x7912`, whose `/` terminator at `0x7976` clears the active
text flag `a5+0x02a6` and text-state flag `a5-0x8e58`. It does not set the
separate phase-exit flag `a5+0x03c2`, so completing this opening message is
not evidence for an early transition to message `0x40`. The catalog validates
the task dispatch and terminator bytes. The text uses the
source ASCII glyphs, palette group 3, and decoded destination `(5,13)`; text
wraps at the 40-column Genesis display edge. Palette 1 is restored to Willow's
actor colors when the message ends. The bounded Window overlay and font
loading are native SGDK code; no arcade CPU code executes in the ROM.
Pixel-for-pixel parity of the CPS text compositor and dialogue background
treatment still needs visual verification.
`make story-catalog` generates `build/willow_story.h` directly from the
assembled source image. It byte-validates the timer/task setup, generic text
dispatch and terminator, and destination pointer before emitting the string,
70-tick delay, 29-tick controller timer interval, palette, and cell
coordinates; the release target depends on this header.

The charged primary child is the queue-class-8 actor created at `0xcba6`.
Its behavior byte `+32` maps through `0xcc50` to selector 1 and byte `+33`
retains that selector; its actual class-8 handler is `0xec84`, not the
profile-1 class-4 handler at `0x115ee`. The class-8 actor's 64-tick movement
and pool reuse are modeled as described above. The separate profile-1 route
remains cataloged but is not linked to this charge child.

The held-charge path at `0xc6c0` allocates from the 20-record, 64-byte
class-2 pool at `a5+0x18c6`, setting behavior byte `+32` to zero. The native
runtime dispatches these records through the source behavior-0 lifecycle at
`0xfb7c`: source slot order, Stage 0 target-relative placement, RNG consumption,
timer expiry, and return to the free-slot stack are implemented. The animation
catalog exports their per-sequence frame codes and holds, and the native
renderer streams those uncompressed frames into Genesis VRAM. The dispatcher
and state handler instruction ranges are byte-checked in the object catalog.
The animation catalog now also byte-verifies the 16 signed spawn coordinate
pairs at `0xfb90` and the four lifetime values `[9, 16, 7, 24]` at `0xfc60`,
then emits them for the native state-zero setup instead of duplicating the
values in runtime code.
The class-2 behavior-1 child allocated at `0xcc28` is linked to the
queue-class-8 allocation at `0xcba6`; native dispatch follows the `0xfe3e`
eight-tick animation and pool-return path. The profile-1 class-4 lifecycle
belongs to a different actor path. The Stage 0 type-2 actor follows the class-12
three-frame animation loop described above. Its native update now checks helper
`0x21c6` on the source 16-frame cadence against the moving camera retirement
bound, then performs the source state-6 cleanup on the following update. The
renderer also uses the source `0x2244` visibility bounds described above.
The separate branch at `0xa1b8` is selected only when the stage field at
`a5+0x0344` equals 4; it allocates objects and writes `0x20`, `0x22`, and
`0x21` to their byte `+32`; it explicitly assigns `(112, 72)` to the `0x22`
object and `(272, 80)` to the `0x21` object, and assigns no coordinates to the
`0x20` object in this block. These are Stage 4 objects, not evidence for the Stage 0 type-2 actor, which
dispatches through class 12 to behavior handler `0x3257e`.

`make object-catalog` writes `build/willow_objects.json`, a static inventory of
94 calls to the arcade object's free-list allocator at `0x2b9c`. The main
dispatcher at `0xffa2` calls all 50 object handlers; each handler can call the
queue builder at `0x2244`, which filters active objects by screen bounds, then uses
the byte at decimal offset `+30` (`0x1e`) to select a class-specific list; it
does not run actor behavior. The catalog labels immediate writes to that byte
as `queue_class`, resolves byte `+32` through the verified 35-entry behavior
table at `0xffc8`, and records the active type and X/Y fields. Handler
addresses alone do not classify an actor as an enemy, projectile, or effect.
The enemy handler uses the byte at
offset `+33` as a collision mode; the catalog records that byte without
assuming all objects share that meaning. It also recognizes direct copies from
the parent's X/Y fields. Of 94 allocation sites, eight write both coordinates
explicitly and 56 copy both from their parent; the latter still need parent
identity and position flow resolved. No explicit queue-class write was found in the
96-byte blocks scanned after these allocations; this does not rule out indirect
or later state assignment. The catalog keeps
the `0xa1b8` records visible but does not classify them as enemies. The nearby
`0xa2a6` record creates active type 1, writes `3` to byte `+32`, and assigns
coordinates `(160, 80)`, matching the player's rendered screen anchor. This
supports its identification as Willow; the type-2 record immediately before
it is the opening class-12 actor at `0xa28a`, with byte `+32 = 1` selecting
handler `0x3257e`. The separate `0x115ee` profile-1 behavior is used by
charge-created children, but its class-4 pool trace does not establish another
Stage 0 spawn.

Per-call field attribution is provisional when a routine allocates multiple
objects before initializing them. At `0x32710` and `0x32716`, the second
allocator call occurs before either object's fields are written, so the simple
scan can attach the first object's fields to the second call. The aggregate
counts above are scan results, not a resolved spawn list.

Further tracing found candidate actor spawns with metadata used by the native
enemy state model. The parent behavior at `0x27faa` allocates an active type 1
object with byte `+32` set to 0 and byte `+33` set to 4 every 16 updates, then
positions it from one of eight relative offsets in the table at `0x28030`. It also queues
sound command `0x33` through `0x786a`; the audio command tables map it to cue
address `0x8f90` (bank 1 ROM offset `0xcf90`). The offline decoder reaches
four active fixed-ROM tracks at `0x004d`, `0x0009`, `0x0600`, and `0x4dff`.
The first three stop at unresolved control events `0x11`, `0x18`, and `0x17`;
track 7 remains in note events through the bounded decode limit. This command
is a sequenced cue, so the native direct-OKI dispatcher cannot play it. Related allocations occur at
`0x2b1c8`, `0x2c2e6`, `0x2c3c4`, `0x2c414`, `0x33152`, and `0x37ade`. These
records are useful leads because the generic enemy logic reads byte `+33` as
its collision mode, but they do not identify a Stage 0 spawn: their parent
objects, event conditions, and handler dispatch still need to be traced before
they can drive the native game.

The object catalog now extracts an additional camera-gated batch at `0x2d550`.
When its manager's world X reaches the camera X, it pops records from the
60-record, 64-byte queue-class-14 pool and initializes active behavior-selector-1
actors. The fixed table at `0x2d586` has 86 six-byte records and a `0xffff`
sentinel; 81 begin in behavior 6 and five in behavior 7. Their X coordinates
span 7,840–14,368, outside the initial 4,096-pixel Stage 0 map window. The
batch and trigger bytes are validated and exported in
`camera_triggered_actor_batch` in `build/willow_objects.json`. Its manager
handler is absent from the 35-entry normal active-record dispatch table at
`0xffc8`, so it does not run as an ordinary actor selected by byte `+32` in
the main pool. Its owning scheduler or stage-entry route remains unresolved;
these actors remain later-stage candidates and are not created in native
Stage 0 gameplay. The catalog also checks all `JSR abs.l`/`JMP abs.l` operands:
the only direct absolute transfer to loader `0x2d550` is the trigger handler's
tail jump at `0x30f78`, and there are none to manager entry `0x30ed0`. This
does not cover PC-relative branches or computed tables. The manager's own
state dispatcher is computed, so its owning actor creation or scheduler still
must be identified through indirect dispatch or stage data before this batch
can be connected to native progression.

A parent chain for the recurring spawner is now byte-validated. The creator at
`0x2fb92` allocates main-pool behavior 20 at its caller's coordinates after
vertical movement and a nonzero result from collision helper `0x3c48`; it also
sets global byte `a5+0x8f0a`. The queue-class-6 scheduler at `0x2f34c` maps
selector 2 to handler `0x2f740`. Its state-2 route reaches `0x2f864`, which
dispatches actor byte `+3` through the PC-relative table at `0x2f8a8`; the
state-6 entry calls `0x2fad0`. That routine dispatches byte `+4` through
`0x2faf2`, where state 6 reaches the collision-and-spawn handler at `0x2fb60`.
The nested queue-class-6 route is byte-validated. No direct branch or call to
`0x2fad0` appears in the assembled program; it is reached through computed
dispatch. The selector-2 actor's creation site remains unresolved, so this
chain is not yet connected to Stage 0. The
handler at `0x1b268` has two child routes (`0x1b2a2` and `0x1b660`) that jump
to `0x49e6`, creating main-pool behavior 15 with a pointer back to the parent.
Behavior 15's handler at `0x18bd8` can create the queue-class-10 selector-9
manager at `0x18e82`; that manager dispatches to `0x27f40` and attempts generic
enemy creation every 16 updates. This links previously separate source paths,
but the actor that reaches creator `0x2fb92` has not been tied to normal Stage 0
setup, so native gameplay still does not spawn this chain.

Two additional behavior-20 creation sites feed the queue-class-10 pool, which
has its own 20-record dispatcher at `0x23516` and selector table at `0x2353c`;
selector 20 resolves to handler `0x26a1c`. The wave creator at `0x26a64`
reserves a linked set of secondary-pool records and positions them from the
parent's direction and a wave-size field. The timed creator at `0x2c150`
allocates the same selector after a two-count, ten-tick state-2 sequence and
uses the parent's direction and subtype for its offset. Both contexts are now
byte-validated in `build/willow_objects.json`. Their parent activation paths
are still not linked to the initial Stage 0 setup, so these records remain
evidence for secondary-pool behavior rather than verified Stage 0 enemies.
I also checked three dynamic selector sources that the immediate-allocation
scan misses: the stage-indexed selector at `0x2f72` yields 0 or 4, the timed
wave table at `0x14264` yields 0, and the queue-class-10 random table at
`0x14842` yields 1–3. None seeds selector 20. This narrows those paths but
does not rule out other computed selector writes or reused pool records.

Four additional paths write selector 9, but the selector is pool-specific.
At `0x15b82`, pool class 4 resolves through the 35-entry behavior table to
`0x15832`. At `0x18e82` and `0x194f0`, allocator `0x2b4e` takes a record from
the 20-entry, 64-byte pool at `0x47c6` (queue class 10); that pool's separate
manager table resolves selector 9 to `0x27f40`. The `0x18e82` path places the
record at parent X/Y minus `(16,24)`. The `0x194f0` path applies the same
offset and may add 32 to X based on a facing flag. The fourth path, at
`0x1a64a`, takes a record from the 60-entry queue-class-12 pool; that pool's
table at `0x2f3c4` resolves selector 9 to `0x1a6d4`. These are separate from type-0 children
created by `0x27196` and `0x33b68`. The catalog preserves the source contexts
and pool identities in `build/willow_objects.json`. The parent records for the
two manager-pool paths are not yet linked to the normal Stage 0 setup, so the
spawner remains disabled in the native runtime.

The class-12 selector-9 handler is now traced: it initializes a 24-tick timer,
applies a timed vertical movement step, advances through its completion state,
then clears its active record through `0x2bb8`. It is a transient actor path,
not the recurring enemy spawner; the latter is selector 9 in queue class 10
and dispatches to `0x27f40`.

The object catalog now validates two additional behavior-0 child creation
paths. The helper at `0x27196` copies its parent's position, selects subtype 4
or 5, adds independently randomized offsets, and then adds 48 pixels to Y.
Its known caller at `0x2712e` fires on a six-tick timer, decrements a parent
spawn counter, selects the subtype from the LFSR, and calls the helper at
`0x27150`. The caller belongs to the queue-class-18 selector-0 manager: its
state-2 handler reaches state 4, where substate 4 runs the timed spawner.
The Stage-counter-3 branch can create that manager through handler `0x1432c`
and creator `0x14a20`; its normal Stage 0 activation remains unproven. State 4
can also be entered directly by the manager's attached behavior-10 child:
after its byte `+42` reaches zero, handler `0x165d2` sets the manager to state
4/substate 2 and activates the attached behavior-11 child. The child starts
with `+42=32`; the exact writer and call path that lower it to zero are still
unresolved. I ruled out the first apparent writer: collision scan `0x37b5e`
visits the twenty 64-byte records initialized as queue class 8 at `0x26f2`,
separate from the child's queue-class-14 pool. A second scan at `0x3a42c` does
walk the active class-4 list, but dispatches inner actor types through a map
at `0x3a4e6`; behavior type 10 maps to `0xff`, so it is skipped before the
collision callback. The nearby callbacks that alter `+42` therefore do not
explain this child's `32 → 0` transition. Its exact writer and call path remain
unresolved, and the native runtime does not infer or simulate the transition.
The linked behavior-11 sibling's zero branch at `0x16706` signals manager
state 4/substate 2 and activates the manager's `+64` child; later manager
shutdown at `0x27102` only sets state 6 on its `+70` and `+64` children. Those
linked-child paths do not write behavior-10's `+42` either.
The
separate helper `0x27048` gate uses parent byte `+52`, whose writer is also
unresolved. The native runtime does not yet run this later-stage manager path.
The path at `0x33b68` selects subtype 2 and spawns at a randomized parent
offset while its parent counts down by one every two updates from 40. Both
dispatch through handler `0x10054`, but neither parent activation is linked to
the initial Stage 0 setup, so these traces do not yet enable an enemy spawn in
the native runtime.

The object catalog also validates three parent-actor creation routes at
`0x49e6`, `0x4a0a`, and `0x255ac`. They allocate selector 15 or 16 from the
60-record queue-class-12 pool. That pool has its own dispatcher at `0x2f39e`
and handler table at `0x2f3c4`: selector 15 resolves to `0x30116`, and selector
16 to `0x368ea`. The first route sets byte `+32` to 15, the second also sets
byte `+33` to 2, and the third sets byte `+32` to 16. This distinction matters
because these selector values do not use the ordinary 35-entry actor table.
The selector-15 handler initializes vector `0xed078` and follows a parent;
selector 16 sets global flag `a5+0x03e3` before its timed sequence; selector 18
copies byte `+48` from its parent and follows the parent's coordinates. These
handler entries are now source-byte validated. Their callers and Stage 0
activation remain unverified.

Selector 16's global flag is read by the generic enemy handler at `0x10054`.
Its code at `0x1136` advances a substate when the flag is set; `0x11e4` holds
while it remains set; the state-4 path at `0x1210` clears it, and `0x1216`
rechecks it before returning to that state. These writer and consumer bytes are
now validated together in the object catalog. This connects the class-12 actor
to generic enemy interaction logic, but still does not establish a Stage 0
creator for either side of the interaction.

The class-12 selector-16 route has an additional verified gate: the manager
state case at `0x2557e` computes `(a5+0x19 + d7) & 3`; when nonzero it calls `0x36f4`
and creates the class-12 selector-16 actor at `0x255ac` only when that helper
returns negative. If the low two bits are zero, it skips that call and may call
`0x2162` when the low three bits are zero, then returns to the shared
scheduler. The catalog validates these branch
bytes. This explains the local activation condition, but does not identify the
manager's Stage 0 creator or establish that this route runs during Stage 0.

I traced one creator upstream: `0x27d2e` allocates selector 11 from the
queue-class-10 pool, which dispatches to `0x25552`. Its parent counts down a
20-tick timer before each attempt, copies its X/Y to the new record, and writes
the computed direction into byte `+15`. The catalog now validates this
allocation site and records its pool and dispatch target. The parent object's
own creation and its connection to Stage 0 remain unverified, so the route is
still not activated in the native game.

In the same source flow, `0x27cda` allocates selector 18 from the
queue-class-12 pool, copies the caller's position, and stores the caller pointer
at byte `+38`. The class-12 table resolves it to `0x369e4`; it does not use the
ordinary selector-18 handler `0x1a4e2`. This adds a verified actor creation
route to the chain, but the flow's entry point still has not been linked to the
normal Stage 0 initializer.

The preceding behavior-14 state path also creates manager selector 7 at
`0x17b3a`. State 2 starts a 42-tick timer; state 4 counts it down, then the
next state allocates from queue class 10 and dispatches to `0x27bd8`. It places
the record using the parent's direction table plus eight pixels of Y offset
and retains the parent pointer at `+38`. Source bytes for this path are now
validated in the object catalog. The creator of that behavior-14 parent is
still not tied to the normal Stage 0 setup.

Four selector-14 actor creation sites are now byte-validated in the object
catalog: `0x1f5d6` in queue class 10, `0x216b0` in queue class 4, and
`0x2f7c8`/`0x34bf6` in queue class 12. Their selectors dispatch to different
handlers by pool: `0x28c7c` for the class-10 manager and `0x176f6` for the
queue-class-4 actor pool, and `0x2ff06` for queue class 12. The last site also
creates queue-class-12 selector 13 (`0x2fdc8`).
Their positions and mode fields are preserved in `build/willow_objects.json`,
but none of these parent creation contexts identifies the initial Stage 0
spawn. This keeps the behavior-14 chain separate from verified Stage 0 data.

The sample extractor decodes the MSM6295's signed 12-bit ADPCM output with
the MAME step formula evaluated as exact integer ratios, at the 1 MHz / 132 rate (about 7,575.76 Hz), then resamples XGM assets to 14 kHz with a
normalized 24-lobe Blackman-windowed sinc filter. It preserves source duration and pitch while improving the
frequency response over nearest-neighbor or linear upsampling; the recording
itself remains limited by the arcade sample data. The extractor also checks
that Z80 startup at `0x0070` copies the value 1 from `0x0e6f` to the OKI pin-7
latch at `0xf006`, so the generated rate matches Willow's configured divider.
Startup now loads SGDK's XGM driver and registers the 40 uncompressed sample
assets as XGM PCM SFX. This supports four overlapping channels and permits
future XGM music to play at the same time. Playback checks each requested
voice channel first, preserving the MSM6295 behavior of ignoring starts on
occupied voices. The direct command table routes all 40 valid samples across
OKI voice 1 or 2; the native build contains a 16 kHz signed 8-bit clip for each
route and maps source attenuation steps to PCM4 volume levels. When XGM and its
PCM channels are idle, the native path starts SGDK's four-channel PCM4 driver
and assigns each source OKI voice to its own channel, preserving simultaneous
two-voice playback. A start on an occupied source voice is ignored, as on the
arcade. While PCM4 runs, XGM is stopped; when it finishes, the native path
restores the mapper and reloads XGM. If XGM music or PCM is already active,
commands use the registered 14 kHz XGM asset so they can mix. Sample `0x19`
has a separate half-gain XGM version for its source volume. The 16 kHz PCM4
rate is an output format choice; the source recordings remain bandwidth-limited
by OKI's roughly 7.576 kHz playback rate. PCM4's length field counts 256-byte
units, so the native sample list passes each clip's zero-padded length rounded
up to a 256-byte boundary; without that padding, the driver would truncate the
last partial block. The PCM4 pack also contains a dedicated half-gain variant
for sample `0x19`; verified direct commands use attenuation level 2, so command
playback selects the pre-attenuated clip at full PCM4 gain instead of quantizing
the source gain to a driver volume step. The asset browser continues to select
the full-level PCM4 sample for audition. The
soundtrack and remaining sequenced YM/OKI cues are still not implemented.
The startup cue catalog now traces the two nonzero pointers that begin in
unmapped Z80 space (`0xff06` and `0xe100`) under MAME's default-zero reads.
Each update consumes a zero control event and a zero operand; after 125 and
3,968 updates respectively, the final reads at `0xfffe/0xffff` leave the track
pointer at zero, so the scheduler skips it on the next update. These tracks
produce no note events in that MAME path and are no longer treated as missing
banked data. Physical open-bus behavior remains unverified. The other active
startup tracks still contain unresolved extended controls, so this trace does
not yet provide a complete native soundtrack.
The pinned SGDK checkout includes MiniMusic, a native Z80
YM2612 player with a compact sequence format and a 6 KiB total data limit.
Its format could host a converted cue, but it replaces the currently used XGM
driver and its playback data must fit in Z80 RAM; adopting it would require
resolving the arcade stream controls, translating instruments and pitches,
and preserving concurrent PCM voice behavior. The native build still uses
XGM for PCM and does not link MiniMusic.
The audio catalog now also extracts the 97-entry source note-index to
YM2151-keycode table at sound-ROM address `0x0b36`. Its bounds and bytes are
validated against the Z80 note lookup path before the generated header exports
it. This is a pitch-data prerequisite for a native YM2612 music converter; it
does not yet decode instrument envelopes or reproduce sequenced music. The
sequencer catalog records all 16 verified control-event dispatch targets at
`0x0952`, together with operand counts and handler effects. Its offline track
decoder now follows event `0x02` using the byte-validated handler at `0x0998`:
it tracks state `+0x0d`, follows the encoded little-endian pointer, and skips
the pointer when the repeat count expires. For example, cue `0x31` track 6
loads repeat value `0xf0` at `0x008b`, jumps to fixed-ROM address `0x0016`, and
then reaches unresolved event `0x11` at `0x0040`. Control event `0x0f` has been
byte-validated as the cue terminator: it unwinds event dispatch and enters the
sound driver's cleanup path. For the source-verified gameplay
cues `0x2a`, `0x2b`, `0x31`, `0x34`, and `0x44`, the
catalog now emits bounded per-track event prefixes with raw note fields,
duration bits, timing values, and control operands. Decoding stops at dynamic
control events not yet traced or after its event cap; these prefixes are source
analysis data, not native music playback. Cue `0x34` is instruction- and caller-validated
at the Stage 0 state-6 timer expiry before the class-10 effect allocation. Its
track-2 prefix reaches control event `0x11` after note `0x47` and timing event
`0x28`. The validated note helper returns with `C=1`, and event `0x28` preserves
that register, so the extended handler's `INC C` makes `C=2` and falls through
to `0x3e21`. This is now recorded for both verified cue-`0x34` call sites.
The normal Stage 0 controller queues cue `0x13`, which resolves to the same
sequence at `0x8f90` as cue `0x33`. Its track 7 has a complete bounded decode:
308 events ending at terminator `0x0f` at sound-ROM offset `0x4f74`. Tracks
2, 5, and 6 stop at extended control events `0x11`, `0x18`, and `0x17`; tracks
1 and 3 point into unmapped sound-CPU space. Startup track 2 now has a verified
entry trace for its `0x11`: note `0x4d` leaves C=1, then timing `0x21` and
control `0x00` preserve C, so `INC C` yields 2 and execution falls through to
`0x3e21`. The rest of that dispatch remains unresolved, and the complete mix
still cannot be recreated from the current decoder.
For startup track 5's event `0x18`, the computed target `0x3a1d` is now traced
through its 74-byte straight-line prefix. When the preceding `0xfb` note
reaches the YM update path, its final register write leaves `C=1`; the target's
37 `INC C` operations and `DEC C` leave `C=0x25`, so `RET NZ` at `0x3a71`
returns without a sound-chip write from the control handler. The track resumes
at `0x000b`, reaches event `0x11` at `0x0040`, and follows the already validated
event-11 entry into the unresolved RST-0x38 loop. This conditional trace still
does not reproduce the complete cue or its repeated timer-service effects.
The catalog extracts the 40-byte OPM patch records selected by instrument
event `0x0c` in verified cue prefixes and the decoded Stage 0 startup track,
and emits those bytes with
their source instrument indices into `build/willow_audio.h`. The loader at
`0x0a2f` and `0x0eb0 + index * 0x28` record stride are byte-validated. The
patch writer at `0x0a4c` is now byte-validated, and the JSON catalog derives
each selected patch's source YM2151 register writes: optional LFO writes when
patch byte `+1` bit 7 is set, channel writes based on sound-RAM byte `0xd013`,
and 20 operator-parameter writes from patch offsets `+20..+39`. The source
advances the register base by eight for each value and skips group `0x60` by
adding `0x20`. The note-start path at `0x0623` reads four three-byte groups
from patch offsets `+8..+19`; the byte-validated helper at `0x06ae` combines
those values with live note and track attenuation state before the computed
levels are written to YM2151 registers `0x60 + channel + {0,8,16,24}`. The
first three operators pass limits 7, 5, and 4 through the level writer at
`0x067d`; the fourth skips that comparison. Record byte `+7` is not read by
these two paths. This is still a source YM2151 trace, not a verified YM2612
conversion. The catalog now also emits a YM2612 register seed for each
instrument: it remaps the four operators' corresponding DT/MUL, KS/AR, DR, SR,
and SL/RR fields, plus channel feedback/algorithm and LFO sensitivity
bitfields. It records the per-operator register mapping explicitly: source
YM2151 patch offsets advance by eight register addresses, while YM2612 offsets
advance by four. Parameter register order is retained independently of the
chips' separate key-on mask ordering. The register pairs appear in the
generated header, while the JSON records their source patch and register
offsets for audit.
The source's note-dependent total-level calculation, OPM LFO conversion, DT2
behavior, pitch conversion, and chip envelope differences remain unresolved,
so this seed is not claimed as a sound-accurate patch. The OPM/OPN register
layouts follow MAME's [YM2151 register map](https://github.com/mamedev/mame/blob/master/3rdparty/ymfm/src/ymfm_opm.h)
and [YM2612-family register map](https://github.com/mamedev/mame/blob/master/3rdparty/ymfm/src/ymfm_opn.h).
The Z80 note-level calculator at `0x06ae` is now traced through its helper at
`0x06ef`: the catalog validates and exports its 128-byte note curve at
`0x0718`, the 256-entry nibble-product table at `0x07a4`, and the `RST 0x20`
table-read helper. It records the calculator's nibble arithmetic and
track-attenuation branch, plus the caller's per-operator base-level inputs.
These generated lookup arrays are data only; the native YM2612 runtime still
needs to apply the arithmetic and schedule note writes.
Register
conversion, execution and sound-register effects after `0x3e21`, control byte
`0x1f`, track timing, and YM/OKI playback remain unresolved.
The catalog also records computed destinations for control bytes `0x10`–`0x1f`.
The validated restart-vector path at `0x0950` indexes using the full control
byte, so these values read overlapping code/data after the verified 16-entry
table; some computed destinations fall in banked ROM or sound RAM. Their
destinations are read by the validated RST path and transferred to with
`JP (HL)`; for the fixed-ROM destinations, this establishes the control-flow
target but not that the bytes form a valid event routine. The catalog now
records raw absolute JP/CALL byte
patterns to fixed-ROM candidates without treating them as control-flow proof.
For cue `0x34`, the computed destination of control event `0x11` is fixed-ROM
address `0x3e0b`; the first bytes (`8b65636563656821`) are now preserved in the
catalog along with the fact that the dispatch word overlaps code after the
verified 16-entry table. Both cue-`0x34` call sites reach it on track 2 after
the same note/timing suffix as cue `0x31` track 6, so the catalog validates the
same `C=1` event entry and traces the shared handler through its computed
target. The catalog derives the entry registers from
the validated restart vectors: `A=0x74`, `B=0x11`, `DE=0x0976`, and
`HL=0x3e0b`; the per-track `IX` pointer is preserved, and `RET` would return to
`0x094d`. Its byte-validated prefix computes `A=0xea` with `Z=0`, so the
conditional call at `0x3e1b` is skipped; the next `INC C`/`JR Z` branch reaches
`0x3e81` only when `C` wraps. Cue `0x31` track 6 reaches event `0x11` at
`0x0040` immediately after note `0x47` at `0x003e` and timing event `0x28` at
`0x003f`. The verified note path writes the YM operator values through helper
`0x0117`, which loads `BC=0xf001` and returns with `C=0x01`; the timing handler
preserves `C`. Thus the `INC C` produces `0x02`, and this cue falls through to
`0x3e21`. The sound tick routine at `0x0b97` selects bank 1 before processing
track pointers; the later `0x040c` routine restores bank 0. The fallthrough
arithmetic reaches `RST 0x30` with `A=0xff`, `C=0x1d`, and `HL=0x3e37`; the
restart-vector path reads the indirect target word at `0x3f35` as `0xa4c3`.
Because the target is reached during track processing, it maps to ROM offset
`0xe4c3`, whose bytes are `0xff` filler, or `RST 0x38`. The vector at `0x0038`
disables interrupts, checks YM timer status, conditionally runs its timer
handlers, and ends in `EI; RETI`. That return lands on the next filler byte at
`0xa4c4` in bank 0 or `0xe4c4` in bank 1; both contain `0xff`, so it re-enters
`RST 0x38` rather than resuming the normal event dispatcher. The bank is
selected by bit 0 of `0xf004`, and MAME configures two 16 KiB audio-bank entries
for CPS-1 ([bank switch and configuration in MAME](https://github.com/mamedev/mame/blob/master/src/mame/capcom/cps1.cpp)). Timer A and command handling can change the selected bank, so both return bytes are checked. The effects of timer-handler reentry from this loop remain unresolved. The catalog validates the vector, both bank mappings, and filler bytes along with the preceding stream events.
Control event `0x1f`
computes `0xcdc9`, outside the configured sound
CPU ROM, RAM, and I/O ranges; the MAME map returns its default value for that
address, while physical open-bus behavior is not established. The offline
decoder now reports each computed target's address region and whether its
dispatch word overlaps the verified table, rather than treating either case
as a normal track event. Cue `0x34` remains unresolved pending execution-state
tracing and YM/OKI-to-Genesis playback work.

## Incremental horizontal column staging (2026-10-03)

`src/willow_native_column_stream.h` now stages a 43-column CPU window into
64-column VDP storage. Each call has a cell budget, retains successfully loaded
rows on retry, and releases exactly the rows owned by a cancelled partial
column. It protects the currently published viewport against both CPU-slot
reuse and independent VDP-column aliasing. A large jump can therefore fail
rather than overwrite visible cells; the caller must diagnose a missed deadline
instead of altering the source camera's motion. Vertical transitions still
require separate staging.

`make test-native-column-stream` is included in `test-native-player-input`.
Address/undefined-behavior sanitizer checks pass 69,158 movement updates and
2,992 partial cancellations, including reversals, failure/retry, and protected
large jumps. The source-trace test compares both live CPS maps to independent
original-ROM lookups across frames 1604–1700, using seven near-plane and four
far-plane cells per update. It verifies all visible cells and shared pattern
reference counts. The background-only working set peaks at 1,138 patterns,
with at most nine new patterns per update after initialization. These figures
exclude native HUD, actor, and temporary pin ownership. Evidence is saved in
`build/native-column-stream-verification.log`; the existing background-map
fixture still passes 2,410,408 pair/subtile comparisons after extraction into
`tools/native_background_fixture.h`.

The headless original-instruction oracle for `0x3b880` now covers all 70 Willow
poses at camera X offsets 0, 1, 32, 80, 127, 256, 511, and -32. It confirms
subtraction of the camera word at A5+0x408 before the CPS 64-pixel origin
adjustment and nine-bit wrapping, with unchanged code, attributes, and sprite
budgets. Evidence: `build/player-camera-geometry-verification.log`.

This is not yet connected to horizontal scrolling in the native intro ROM.
Source hardware publication timing, native cache ownership, sprite positioning,
and 68000/DMA frame budgets still need integrated verification. The published
diagnostic ROM is unchanged; these host checks do not establish 60 FPS or a
completed port. All checks above run without emulator windows.


### Original horizontal register publication

`src/willow_arcade_scroll_publication.h` translates the original
`0x197a..0x19b2` horizontal register publication slice: it writes the old
staged words at A5+0x7442/0x7446/0x744a to CPS Scroll1/2/3 X registers, then
stages the source published words at A5+0x2e/0x32/0x36 minus 64, preserving
16-bit wrapping. Source controller publication remains a separate step.
`make test-arcade-scroll-publication` executes the original instructions in
the headless 68000 core and compares 12,288 layer cases, including signed and
wrap boundaries. Only the three hardware destination operands are relocated
to observable RAM; an RTS bounds the isolated slice. Original opcodes and
CPS destinations are checked before relocation. The successful log is
`build/scroll-publication-verification.log`. This verifies register semantics,
not task/VBlank phase alignment; integrated native rendering still needs that
phase comparison before horizontal scrolling is enabled.


### Native horizontal integration in progress

The working `native/intro_probe/src/main.c` now allocates both column states
after the restoration-offset buffer is released, transfers initial column
ownership from rows to column metadata, and connects native load/release
callbacks to the live CPS maps and existing pattern cache. It applies the
preceding horizontal camera publication and subtracts the preceding camera X
from actor screen positions. At the initial stationary origin it uses the
already prepared column 40, avoiding speculative loads during pin retirement.
The integration smoke test now derives ownership, palette, map, and VRAM-byte
expectations from every complete or partial column in both native rings.

The initial native run passed through update 930 with 1,302 free heap bytes
and the same 1,277-pattern peak (`build/native-horizontal-smoke.log`). The
walking run fails at update 935 / emulator frame 1006 with input already
advanced to the next update (`build/native-horizontal-walk.log`): horizontal
work exceeds the available frame budget. This is an unresolved timing failure,
not a passing scrolling release. The published diagnostic remains unchanged.
Backups of the pre-integration runtime and smoke test are
`build/main-before-horizontal.c` and `build/smoke-before-horizontal.c`.
The loader's visible-column scans now advance ring indices rather than divide
for each cell; host sanitizer and original-instruction checks were rerun in
`build/native-horizontal-host-checks.log`. Further 68000 profiling and timing
work are required before integrated scrolling, pixels, or 60 FPS can be claimed.

### Horizontal frame-budget profiling

`debugColumnLines[4]` records entry, completion of each plane, and exit using
SGDK's adjusted V counter. On the first captured walking update, the renderer
enters column work at line 151 and completes the near plane at line 224; the
frame ends while the far plane is still acquiring a cache pattern. The smoke
test reports these counters and the 68000 PC on an input-phase mismatch.
Isolating the bounded-cache acquisition routine saved only about one scanline;
span reuse and broad no-inline changes did not help (the latter also disturbed
intro timing). Gradual stationary preloading still exceeded a frame during
handoff cleanup. Those experiments were removed. The next target is repeated
full-window searches/readiness scans in the column scheduler, with the current
host oracle retained to check all cells independently after optimization.
The native integration remains unpublished and fails the walking timing test.

### Adjacent-column scheduler and VBlank publication

`willowColumnStreamAdjacent` avoids full-window scans when the previous
published viewport is complete, the preceding target equals that viewport,
and the next camera movement is at most eight pixels. Only viewport edges and
up to three guard columns can need work; interior ownership is retained. Larger
moves use the existing general scheduler. A failed call requires re-establishing
the complete-viewport invariant before another fast call. The native caller
reports failures instead of clamping source camera motion.

`make test-native-column-adjacent` runs the same independent full-cell,
reference, cancellation, CPU/VDP alias, and source-map audits for this path.
The sanitizer tests pass 69,158 movement updates with 2,992 partial
cancellations and the 97-frame two-plane source walk. The host oracle still
checks every visible cell; it does not use the fast path's edge-only readiness
criterion to establish correctness. Evidence: `build/native-adjacent-verification.log`.

Native horizontal register changes now use `DMA_QUEUE_COPY` at VBlank.
The integration verifier checks every visible pattern immediately, and checks
new offscreen patterns after their queued upload reaches the next VBlank.
Existing pattern IDs are checked on every sample. This avoids mistaking an
unflushed, safely offscreen DMA request for a rendering error.

The 930-update no-input native regression passes
(`build/native-horizontal-smoke.log`). On the first walking update, near-plane
work now spans lines 151–196 instead of 151–224; both planes complete by line
254. The following update reaches column work at line 180 and still exceeds
the deadline (`build/native-horizontal-walk.log`, last completed update 936).
This is progress on frame cost, not a passing walking or 60 FPS result. The
published diagnostic is unchanged. Further work must reduce worst-case loading
cost and verify phase alignment and actual scrolling pixels before publishing.

### Direct column name-table writes

The streaming callback now writes the VDP control/data ports directly using
the already established 64-column plane geometry and fixed C000/E000 name-table
bases. It emits the same VRAM write command and attribute as SGDK's
`VDP_setTileMapXY`, while avoiding that helper's general plane-address lookup.
The loader still protects published columns before invoking the callback;
pattern uploads and horizontal-scroll changes remain queued for VBlank.

On walking update 936, the adjusted V-counter measurements improve from
151/196/253/254 to 151/191/245/245 (entry/near/far/exit). The following update
still overruns after entering at 180; near-plane completion improves from 252
to 246. These are adjusted V-counter values, not an absolute CPU-cycle profile:
SGDK adds 32 during NTSC active display and maps blanking to 16. Differences
within active display can be compared; values must not be subtracted across
blanking as though they were a monotonically increasing 262-line clock.
The 930-update no-input smoke test passes again. The walking failure and
completed-frame measurements remain in `build/native-horizontal-walk.log`.

Per-cell instrumenting and batched name-table DMA were evaluated and removed:
the instrumentation materially perturbed timing, while DMA copy/queue overhead
made short-column writes slower. The final retained change is the direct
name-table write. No scrolling release or 60 FPS claim is justified yet.

### Retained HUD SAT entries and inline actor assembly

Frame-phase profiling showed substantial time inside actor/SAT assembly, not
just the column loader. The native renderer now retains unchanged HUD entries
in SGDK's sprite cache. Preparation marks all HUD entries dirty; appending a
HUD sprite or moving it into a private tile allocation marks that specific
entry dirty. Actors still start after the current HUD count, and the HUD-to-actor
link is maintained each update. Sprite uploads still occur every update.
Only SAT assembly is skipped for unchanged HUD entries; source HUD state,
compositing, pattern updates, timing, and sprite order are unchanged.

HUD and actor SAT construction now write the same `VDPSprite` fields as
`VDP_setSpriteFull` directly, avoiding repeated call/argument overhead. The
native walking test completes updates 936 through 958 before a later overloaded

100 with the frame profiler enabled. The failure after 958 has phase readings

`make test-native-player-sprites SGDK_ROOT=/tmp/willow-sgdk-resume` passes with

diagnostic remains unchanged pending a complete passing walking/timing check.

### HUD cell index and direct composition into DMA storage

After restoration releases its temporary offset buffer, the native renderer
allocates a 200-byte HUD cell-to-sprite index from the retained sprite layout.
This replaces repeated linear searches during dirty-cell updates. Newly added
HUD sprites update the index; private-tile assignment keeps the same sprite
index. Allocation failure releases the index if column-state allocation fails.
No source HUD values or update timing are changed.

Already-private HUD cells are composed directly into the SDK's queued DMA
buffer with `DMA_allocateAndQueueDma`; other cells retain the original path,
including visibility checking and first-time private tile allocation. This
avoids a second 32-byte copy and repeated private-tile lookup. Immutable sprite
and background pattern uploads call `DMA_queueDma` with the same source,
destination, word count, and stride previously passed through the generic
transfer wrappers.

`make test-native-player-sprites SGDK_ROOT=/tmp/willow-sgdk-resume` passes again
(`build/native-hud-index-regression.log`), including the intro, HUD, palette,
damage, geometry, and 70-pose/3,942,400-pixel checks. The walking trace progresses
through update 966 before a combined camera-map boundary and sprite-upload
frame overruns. Its phase readings are 16/47/102/111/169, with column entry 173
and near completion 230. See `build/native-horizontal-walk.log`. Sustained
walking timing is still failing, and the published ROM remains unchanged.

### Aligned distant-map packed copies

The native distant-map copy callback now copies aligned groups of eight IDs
directly from the generated packed ROM data. Eight 11-bit IDs occupy eleven
bytes, so groups beginning on eight-ID boundaries remain byte-aligned even
when they begin halfway through a word. The big-endian 68000 representation
matches the generated packed words. Range and group-alignment checks precede
the copy; unaligned/partial transfers retain the exact per-ID path.

The new byte-copy audit in `test_arcade_scroll3_map_store.c` serializes words
explicitly in big-endian order and compares all 5,632 destination bytes against
independent per-ID updates. All 4,076 combinations pass, covering both byte
alignments and 8/16/24/64-ID groups. Existing 8,388,608 ID/neighbor checks and the
1,010-frame controller/map trace also pass. `test-intro-probe` passes with zero
intro, player-gate, or HUD pixel mismatches. Evidence:
`build/native-packed-copy-regression.log`.

On the failing walking boundary update, camera-phase completion improves from
adjusted counter 102 to 94, and column work starts at 164 instead of 173.
Walking still fails after completed update 966, so this is not sufficient for
sustained 60 FPS. Experiments with constant-shift strided rows and near-map
memcpy were removed because they did not materially improve that update. The
published diagnostic remains unchanged.

### Passing captured walk after sprite retention and aligned DMA

The two scripted actors retain their SAT geometry when their animation address
and starting SAT index are unchanged. Only coordinate deltas are applied; the
last link is restored before the final chain termination. Culling invalidates
the retained entry, and any animation/index change takes the full construction
path. This optimization starts only after the HUD handoff, preserving the
previously verified intro path.

The pattern resources are now aligned to their DMA block sizes in `probe.res`:
32 bytes for background/overlay patterns and 128 bytes for player sprite
blocks. A block of either size at its matching alignment cannot cross the
Genesis DMA 128 KiB source boundary. Those two upload paths therefore use
`DMA_queueDmaFast`, retaining the SDK's normal queue management. The native
smoke test rejects a ROM whose linked resource symbols violate these alignment
requirements before executing it.

`make test-native-player-input SGDK_ROOT=/tmp/willow-sgdk-resume` now passes
(`build/native-horizontal-full-regression.log`). The captured walk reaches all

player/camera/map states match the captured arcade walk. The same run passes
intro/HUD/palette/damage checks, 70 poses with 3,942,400 matching pixels, and all
5,513 background-bank patterns / 176,416 VRAM bytes. Peak cache residency remains
1,277 patterns; free native heap after handoff is 1,016 bytes. A saved walking
scanout at update 970 was also inspected headlessly.

This establishes timing for the captured walk, not for all input sequences or

### Original visibility queue producers

`willow_arcade_visibility.h` now translates the full producer path at `0x2244`,
`0x2296`, and `0x22dc`, through the selector/lane dispatch at `0x2282..0x2506`.
It preserves inactive actors' previous admission flag, clears active actors'
flag before testing, and sets it only on admission. All three source viewport
biases/limits retain unsigned word arithmetic. Admitted actors select the
original queue using record bytes +30 and +14; the producer decrements the
16-bit queue pointer, stores the actor handle, and increments the byte count
with source wrap behavior. It introduces no capacity clamp absent from source.

The bus interface uses source RAM addresses and 16-bit actor handles. It still
requires a native pool/scheduler adapter; these producers are not yet connected
to the diagnostic ROM. The published diagnostic's scope therefore remains
unchanged. The existing sprite geometry oracle now tests all valid selectors
and lanes, inactive/active flags, camera wrap, and each viewport's exact
boundaries, comparing all RAM below its synthetic return stack against the
original unmodified instructions. The oracle also retains the existing 8,192
ordinary-visibility cases and all 70 poses at eight camera offsets.

The RNG arithmetic itself was already translated in `willow_arcade_services.h`
and exhaustively checked. Connecting only the player callback would not yet
reproduce the shared actor call order: the saved arcade walk trace contains
RNG state `2472/00` at frame 1587 and `c91c/02` at frame 1589. Native integration
must restore the relevant shared scheduling rather than assign a separate
player seed or replay these captured values.

Validation passes with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer:
8,448 queue-producer cases, 8,192 admission cases, and 560 pose/camera cases.
Evidence: `build/source-visibility-queues.log`. All execution was headless.

### Visibility queue initialization and draining

The source does not blanket-clear visibility queues each frame. Initialization
at `27BA`, `28B8`, `290E`, and `2972` installs lane end pointers and writes the
source D1 count byte; the first two tails also write `FFf99d` and `FF83cb`.
`willowArcadeVisibilityInit` now translates these four tails. Its group argument
selects the main pools, class 8, class 14, or class 2 respectively. Normal source
initializer callers supply zero; the translation preserves any supplied byte.

The consumers at `3B642..3B87E` walk queued actor handles in ascending memory
order, rendering each before decrementing the count, and publish the advanced
pointer after the last actor. `willowArcadeVisibilityDrain` preserves that
ordering, including leaving an empty lane untouched. The supplied callback is
the sprite writer; the caller must select the special `3BAA4` writer for class
18 lane 1 on stage 4. That writer and the full renderer dispatch are not
implemented by this drain helper.

### Attract replay state and input routing

`willow_arcade_attract_state.h` translates the original entry prefix at
`8CDA..8D04`, restoration at `8E18..8E2C`, and complete input mux at

original ROM descriptor at `8CCA`, sets the input duration to one, and advances
the manager state. Restoration recovers both saved words, clears player-active,
and updates manager/completion state. The RNG scratch byte is retained.

The input mux copies current to previous before choosing live input or replay.
Live player selection preserves the source second-player/cabinet-bit gate.
Replay duration is a wrapping word countdown; at expiry a zero-duration record
skips exactly one record, then loads its input/duration and advances the pointer.

inputs rather than values learned from video or an emulator capture.

### Task initialization, completion, suspension and reuse

The task-record header now also translates stack-base initialization
(`144E..1464`) from the original `17DC` table and free-slot stack initialization
(`1490..14AA`) from `181C`. The latter pushes eight pointers in the original
order, rather than synthesizing a differently ordered allocator. Completion
(`163A..1656`, `165E..1688`) always clears the current record's payload; dynamic
completion also returns its full source pointer to the free stack. This differs
from external cancellation, which skips inactive records. Suspend/resume
(`17A4`/trap 5, `17C0`/trap 6) preserve payload and saved execution fields.

The oracle compares these record services independently and composes original
initialization, nine allocation attempts (including exhaustion), eight releases
in a permutation, and eight reallocations with RAM preserved between calls.
Completion is entered after the exception-frame discard and stopped before
scheduler context restoration at `151E`; this does not verify the context
switch itself. Initialization similarly stops at the exact boundary before
unrelated startup work. Suspend/resume execute their actual trap wrappers,
register saves and returns. Native cooperative scheduling remains unfinished.

operations, full non-stack RAM comparison, fatal sanitizers, and strict
SGDK/68000 compilation. Evidence: `build/source-task-lifecycle.log`. The
existing `test-arcade-tasks` regression target runs both sets. No GUI was
opened, and the saved diagnostic ROM remains unchanged.

### Asynchronous event command waits

`willowArcadeEventCommandWaitBegin` translates entries 1E88, 1EAA, 1ECC,
1EDE and 1EF0. They set FFF891 to one, enqueue 0C00/0C10/0C1A with either
fixed argument three or caller D0, and unconditionally request a one-tick
sleep. The returned source continuation identifies 1EA2, 1EC4 or 1F0A.
`willowArcadeEventCommandWaitPending` is used after that sleep: any nonzero
flag requests another one-tick sleep, and zero permits the caller to return.
Neither helper consumes the command, clears the flag, or simulates completion.
The native scheduler must supply the suspension; these helpers are not yet
wired into the synchronous event service adapter.

`test-arcade-event-command-wait` passes 20,480 boundary comparisons across
all five entries and 64 canonical queue offsets, with patterned RAM, caller
arguments, initial flags and repeated 80/FF/00 completion-flag transitions.
The original producer executes unchanged. A fixture jump at 1750 stops at
the sleep-service boundary, preserving the original JSR return address; tests
verify D0=1, stack position, continuation, A4 and full non-stack RAM. Resumed
checks start at the original post-sleep instruction. Thus these tests verify
the producer/wait control flow, not task context restoration or the command
consumer. Those remain separate integration requirements. Fatal sanitizers
and strict SGDK/68000 compilation pass. Evidence:
`build/source-event-command-wait.log`. No GUI was launched and no ROM published.

### Queued-command consumer resume and task allocation

`willowArcadeCommandConsumerResume` translates 1E18 through the next yield
at 1E14. It checks inhibit byte FF020E and free-task count FF020C, reads the
entry at FF8072+FF801C, and consumes only a nonnegative command longword.
Consumption writes FFFFFFFF to that entry, wraps the read offset with FC,
and allocates one dynamic task through the translated 160A record service.
The command's high byte is a byte offset into the original longword table
at 1E34; its low byte and argument become the task's two parameter words.
It never drains multiple commands in a single resume or uses the producer
write offset as an empty-queue test.

The following 1DDC conditional wake scan runs when FFF99C is nonzero or when
FF828F is nonzero and FF8068 bit zero is set. It updates the original sixteen
task records, then the caller must yield. This scan is separate from the
VBlank wake scan and must not be arbitrarily merged with it.

`test-arcade-event-command-consumer` passes 16,384 resumes with 9,728 actual
allocations, covering all eight command table families and 64 read offsets,
negative entries, inhibit/exhaustion gates, sleeping task delays and unrelated
RAM preservation. Original trap 7 and allocation execute unmodified with the
appropriate exception vector. Only the 1784 yield entry is replaced by a
fixture stop, preserving its JSR continuation at 1E18. Full non-stack RAM and
the yield stack match. Fatal sanitizers and strict SGDK/68000 compilation pass.
Evidence: `build/source-event-command-consumer.log`.

This verifies allocation and pre-yield memory behavior, not execution of the
allocated handler or scheduler context restoration. Transition family 0C
selects 582C, which dispatches through table 583C; subcommand zero begins at
5858 by enqueueing 1000 and waiting for FF82C0 before clearing CPS surfaces.
Those asynchronous handlers and native scheduler integration remain required.
All validation stayed headless; the native ROM was not republished.

### Transition command 0C10 continuation

`src/willow_arcade_transition.h` translates the 597E handler selected by the
original 582C/583C dispatch for command 0C10. It enqueues 1002 with the task's
low argument byte, unconditionally sleeps one tick, and resumes at 5994.
A nonzero FF82C0 requests another one-tick sleep. Once that word is zero,
it reads the argument byte again and sleeps for that delay, resuming at 59A4.
Only there does it clear FFF891 and request dynamic task completion/release.
The returned continuation/delay/finish result must be honored by the native
scheduler. In particular, delay zero invokes source indefinite suspension;
it is not an instruction to immediately clear the completion flag.

`test-arcade-transition-reveal` passes 16,384 boundary comparisons spanning
all 256 argument bytes, all queue offsets and dynamic slots, initially ready
and busy status words, repeated busy waits, final delays, and flag clearing.
The original dispatch table and command producer execute unchanged. Fixture
stops replace only sleep service 1750 and finish service 165A; continuation
PC, D0 delay, stack boundary and all non-stack RAM are compared. Final
continuation checks are explicit resume fixtures, including delay zero; they
do not claim the scheduler would automatically resume a zero-delay task.
Fatal sanitizers and strict SGDK/68000 compilation pass. Evidence:
`build/source-transition-reveal.log`. The fade task itself, native suspension/
release integration and other transition selectors remain unfinished. No GUI
was launched or focused, and no native ROM was republished.

### Original task-selection scan

`src/willow_arcade_task_scheduler.h` translates 14D8..14FA, selecting the
first task with unsigned state >=4 while scanning upward in 32-byte slots.
It checks FF020E before each slot and returns at the original restart boundary
if inhibited or exhausted. Returned slot and remaining-count values preserve
the source cursor and DBF wrap, including count FFFF at exhaustion. The caller
must perform the separate 14CC restart/clear, interrupt masking, context
dispatch and restoration. The helper deliberately does not silently skip
invalid high states: the arcade also selects them, although only states 4/8/12
have valid context-handler entries.

`test-arcade-task-scheduler` passes 16,384 original-instruction scans: all 256
state bytes, all 16 starting slots, inhibition, exhaustion and later-ready
cases. Results include 8,128 dispatches and 8,256 restarts. Fixture stops are
at 14FA before dispatch and 14CC before restart; the scan is unchanged. Original
PC, A0, D0 (including its preserved high word), selected state and all non-stack
RAM match. Fatal sanitizers and strict SGDK/68000 compilation pass. Evidence:
`build/source-task-scheduler.log`.

This establishes the scan rule needed for native scheduling, but does not yet
replace the explicit order in the composed transition fixture. Interrupt
interleaving, task context restoration and native scheduling remain required.
Validation was headless, with no emulator GUI or ROM publication.

### Task dispatch context, original 1528 / 152E / 153E

`willowArcadeTaskContext` describes the task-owned context selected for states

The result describes arcade context, not executable native entry addresses.

stack in reverse register order; restoration reads ascending register order.
The caller's return address remains above the frame. Yield at 1784 has no
MOVEM wrapper and must not use these helpers; the earlier context note has
been corrected to distinguish it from sleep.

`test-arcade-task-sleep-cycle` passes 4,096 complete original-code cycles:
MOVEM save, TRAP 3 and its original exception handler, context resume through

fifteen registers, task-record writes, saved and returned stack, CCR, and all
RAM outside the six-byte supervisor exception-frame scratch area. All delay
bytes and CCR combinations occur. Only the shared 151E scheduler return is
stopped; the fixture then explicitly resumes the task, including zero-delay
suspended cases. This verifies context round trips, not wake timing or full
scheduler integration. Fatal sanitizers and strict SGDK/68000 compilation
pass. Evidence: `build/source-task-sleep-cycle.log`.

The native runtime still needs continuation binding, scheduler scan/restart
integration, interrupt ordering and frame-budget validation. No GUI was
started, no focus was changed and no ROM was republished.

### Scheduler supervisor-frame round trip

`willowArcadeSchedulerSave` translates 14FA..1506's ten-byte supervisor frame:
return PC 14EC, low-word scan counter, and full task pointer. It publishes the
saved stack at FF0200 and current task at FF0204. `willowArcadeSchedulerRestore`
translates 151E..1526, reloading that saved stack independently of the active
task stack and returning its cursor, counter, PC and final stack pointer.
The caller must preserve D0's current upper word when applying the restored
counter; the arcade only restores the low word.

`test-arcade-scheduler-return` passes 12,288 round trips across all three valid
dispatch states, all slots, varied counters and supervisor stacks. The actual
save/restore instructions execute unchanged. Only the dispatch table targets
are redirected to a fixture stop, and 14EC stops before continuing the scan.
The test compares active stack, current-task pointer, restored cursor/count,
return target and every RAM byte, including the entire saved frame. It changes
the active stack and D0 upper word before restoration to verify that the saved
scheduler stack is used and the upper word is not restored. Fatal sanitizers
and strict SGDK/68000 compilation pass. Evidence:
`build/source-scheduler-return.log`.

These helpers describe the source scheduler state; complete scan/task/wake
integration and native continuation binding remain unfinished. Validation was
headless and the native diagnostic ROM was not republished.

`src/willow_native_task_store.h` provides an 820-byte source-addressed store:

and original pointer values. Other globals and task stacks are explicitly
unmapped, allowing a runtime adapter to route them to their actual owners.
No invented initialization is applied. Unsupported word accesses return
failure, preserve the output value on reads, and do not partly write.

assertion. Evidence: `build/native-task-store.log`.

opened and no native ROM was republished.

`src/willow_native_task_runtime.h` supplies a 32-byte per-slot continuation

source task allocation/state fields, byte delays, current-task pointer and
dynamic release service. Native continuation labels replace source CPU stacks
for these bodies; task +4/+8 CPU-context fields are not repurposed or claimed
to match a running arcade CPU. Fresh state 12 overrides stale labels, yield
preserves the delay byte, and sleep zero becomes indefinite state 2.
Unsupported states, entries or selectors are reported before mutation.

sanitizers and strict SGDK/68000 compilation pass, with a 32-byte size check.
Evidence: `build/native-task-runtime.log`. The underlying routines have their
separate source instruction oracles; this native integration test is not yet
a differential comparison of the full dispatcher with original scheduler

`build/native-task-runtime-target.log`.

renderer and VDP work. This is affirmative evidence that the current generic
per-word palette callback path is unsuitable for a 60 FPS game loop. Passing
behavioral tests does not make this implementation ready for publication.
The probe's extra palette/global storage also is not a demonstrated fit in
the diagnostic's free heap. Palette representation/write cost and runtime RAM
ownership must be resolved before connecting this path to gameplay. Native
continuation semantics themselves match, but performance integration remains
unfinished. All execution stayed headless; no ROM was republished.

### Bulk palette-group update path

The fade primitive now accepts an optional `adjustGroup` callback that adds the
original delta to exactly sixteen contiguous words after the original first-
color brightness test. Mask updates, group order, word wrap, asymmetric last
two banks and completion sums remain unchanged. Existing callers retain the
per-word callback path. The task adapter/native dispatcher expose grouped
variants, with compatibility wrappers for existing callers.

The target runtime probe supplies a direct contiguous-word group updater,
unrolled across the fixed sixteen colors, while its host comparison deliberately
uses the old per-word path. All 520 target scan/wake passes still match. The
worst isolated pass falls from eight emulated slices to two with the grouped
path; final timing evidence is `build/native-task-runtime-grouped-unrolled.log`.
The full source palette oracle also passes both callback modes: each verifies
6,144 arithmetic/group cases and 2,304 task yield/exit boundaries, including
mixed color brightness, all masks and all 3,072 palette words. Evidence:
`build/source-palette-grouped.log`.

This is an output-preserving optimization, not permission to apply a tint or
lower RGB precision. Two elapsed emulator slices still do not establish a
one-frame game budget, and renderer/VDP work is absent. Palette RAM ownership
and further performance work remain necessary before runtime integration.
No GUI was used and the diagnostic ROM was not republished.

### Calibrated CPU-cycle profile and aligned task-word access

The target continuation harness now supports `--cycles`, executing one CPU
instruction at a time through the core's exported `m68k_run` API. Its local
core-state prefix is validated against PC and all sixteen public register
reads before use; a NOP calibration requires exactly 28 master cycles (four
68000 cycles). The profile resets cycle/refresh phase for each pass and includes
the core's bus-refresh charges. This is isolated CPU execution: VDP/DMA,
contention, renderer and game workload are not modeled by this timing mode.

The grouped updater's byte-wise bus adapter measured 928,508 master cycles
(132,644 CPU cycles) at worst. Using a single aligned native word access for
the verified task routines' aligned, within-region word addresses reduces this
to 766,864 master cycles (109,552 CPU cycles), with at most 8,561 instruction
steps. The host deliberately retains byte-wise access for comparison. All
520 passes match in both normal emulator and cycle modes, and normal execution
now needs at most one emulator frame call per isolated pass. Evidence:
`build/native-task-runtime-word-profile.log`.

The aligned fast path is confined to the target fixture adapter; the general
compact-store boundary-checking API remains intact. These results identify a
usable access strategy for eventual native integration, not proof that the
full game fits 60 FPS. Palette storage and remaining gameplay work still need
RAM and timing integration. No GUI was launched or focused.

### Exact packed brightness-offset palette experiment

`src/willow_native_palette_view.h` represents group brightness adjustments with
96 bytes (192 packed nibbles) over base CPS words supplied by a separate owner.
Reads add the group's modulo-16 brightness offset; individual writes subtract
it before forwarding the exact word to that owner. It preserves all twelve
RGB bits and each color's independent original brightness. Group adjustments
reject non-brightness deltas and invalid addresses without mutation. It does
not yet provide a ROM-backed mutable palette owner or eliminate base storage.

`test-native-palette-view` passes 6,144 mixed fade/write steps comparing every
one of 3,072 colors plus all masks/sums; it also checks all 192 groups and 16
offsets, neighbor-nibble preservation and rejected operations. Fatal sanitizers
pass. An optional compiled target probe (`test-native-task-runtime-lazy`)
compares decoded target colors against the host's materialized palette over
520 scheduler passes. Both normal and calibrated cycle modes match.

The first compiled version cost 155,630 cycles at worst; narrower address
arithmetic and simpler packed-nibble updates reduce it to 134,944. This is
still slower than direct grouped writes at 109,552. Therefore direct writes
remain the default target probe, and the offset representation stays isolated
behind `WILLOW_PROBE_LAZY_PALETTE` for future RAM ownership work. Evidence:
`build/native-palette-view.log`, `build/native-task-runtime-lazy-final.log`,
and `build/native-task-runtime-direct-retained.log`. This experiment is not a
60 FPS improvement or a completed palette-memory solution. No GUI was used.

### ROM palette base-source ownership

`src/willow_native_palette_sources.h` maps each of 192 sixteen-color groups
to a ROM word offset relative to E0000, using 384 bytes. FFFF marks an unowned
group, which must be resolved by a separate preserved/mutable owner; reads
report failure rather than inventing colors. Stage binding follows the five
copy ranges in 0978..0A10, retaining the unselected half of bank three and
banks four/five. All source ranges are validated before changing mappings.
This does not implement arbitrary palette writes or animation's brightness-OR
copies, and it has not replaced the diagnostic renderer's palette ownership.

`test-native-palette-sources` passes all 49 ordered stage transitions, with
98 full comparisons of 3,072 words against the existing source-verified stage
initialization helper, including unchanged groups seeded from different ROM
sources. Unowned reads preserve their output and invalid stage/range bindings
are rejected. Fatal sanitizers and strict SGDK/68000 compilation pass, with
a 384-byte size assertion. Evidence: `build/native-palette-sources.log`.

The source map plus 96-byte brightness view is 480 bytes before mutable
exceptions; together with task storage/continuations this exceeds the last
measured free heap. Dynamic palette ownership and memory reclamation still
need implementation. This establishes exact ROM ownership for stage copies,
not a completed memory solution or visual check. No GUI was opened.

### Composed ROM palette ownership

`src/willow_native_palette_owner.h` combines the 384-byte ROM source map with
96 bytes of brightness offsets. Reads retain every original CPS RGB bit.
Stage installation follows the source-verified 0978..0A10 helper, resets
brightness offsets only for copied groups, and preserves the other groups.
The C92 copy adapter computes all sixteen results using the original OR of
source words with retained destination brightness. It publishes a new ROM
binding only when every resulting word is represented exactly by one shared
brightness offset; otherwise the complete previous owner remains untouched.
Unowned and invalid reads/copies fail rather than inventing colors.

`test-native-palette-owner` passes fatal sanitizers, all 49 ordered stage
transitions (98 complete 3,072-word comparisons), and 8,192 copy cases against

all representable; mixed ROM regions produce 5,400 exact bindings and 2,792
atomic rejections overall. Neighbor groups remain unchanged. Invalid stage,
address, range and unowned-copy checks pass. Strict SGDK/68000 compilation
passes with a 480-byte size assertion. Evidence: `build/native-palette-owner.log`.

This owner is not yet connected to the diagnostic or task dispatcher. It does
not implement arbitrary palette writes or storage for unrepresentable groups;

### Mutable palette exceptions and captured storage bounds

`src/willow_native_palette_mutable.h` adds caller-owned 34-byte exception

one word. Shared brightness offsets still work with mixed base brightness.
C92 copies preserve each word's destination brightness; a representable result
returns to ROM ownership and frees its exception slot. Stage copies retire
only the replaced groups. Explicit whole-group installation can initialize
known data; single writes to unowned groups fail instead of inventing the
other fifteen colors. Exhaustion is a failure before mutation, not a dropped
write that the caller may ignore.

`test-native-palette-mutable` passes fatal sanitizers with 8,192 interleaved
operations and 25,165,824 word comparisons against materialized colors:

slot reuse and stage retirement. Strict SGDK/68000 compilation also passes.

70 mutable groups; this is not an estimate of gameplay requirements.

`tools/palette_owner_probe.c` runs the owner as compiled 68000 code in the

helpers. This is compiled-representation validation, not a new end-to-end

Initial target costs exposed repeated ownership searches inside sixteen-word

mutable slots without additional RAM. ROM-only reads reject those tags.
Larger exception pools keep the exact bounded-search fallback. The host's
192-slot mixed tests exercise that fallback as well as the direct tags;
invalid-tag ROM reads leave their output unchanged.

The final fixture's worst costs in 68000 cycles are: initialization 45,342;
individual write 3,108 (initially 16,908); C92 copy 5,652 (initially 17,000);
brightness adjustment 630; stage install 42,072; individual read 826.
The profiler validates the local core register-layout view and a four-cycle
NOP before measuring. Figures include bus refresh, exclude VDP/DMA contention
and all game/renderer workload, and do not prove 60 FPS. All host sanitizers,

### Native overlay run storage (2026-10-03)

The native intro now stores one `overlayFirstSlot` instead of 184 duplicated
attributes. A headless audit of the published baseline showed its overlay
patterns occupy a consecutive cache run (slots 475..658). The implementation
does not hardcode those addresses: it records the first actual allocation and
checks every following allocation against that base plus the pattern index.
Nonzero attributes reconstruct the same priority, palette and slot bits;
pattern zero stays blank. Retirement releases the same descending slots.
The host smoke oracle independently compares every loaded pattern's inverse
cache mapping against the recorded base on each update.

A first attempt to look up each pattern in the general cache failed the intro
frame checks and was set aside (`build/main-overlay-cache-experiment.c`). The
consecutive-run representation avoids those lookups as well as the duplicate
RAM. The native smoke run verifies 930 source updates with zero missed updates
or cache overflows, all actor records, tile ownership and handoff state.
Measured free heap rises from 1,036 to 1,400 bytes; allocator alignment makes
the net recovery 364 bytes. A read-only walk of heap metadata reports a largest
coalesced run of 1,162 bytes, including allocator headers. Thus the total does
not imply a contiguous 1,400-byte runtime allocation is possible.

Evidence: `build/intro-overlay-slot-layout.log` and `.txt`,
`build/native-overlay-contiguous-run.log`, and
`build/native-overlay-heap-audit.log`. The full target passed in
`build/native-overlay-run-regression.log`, including intro/gate/HUD checks,
all 70 poses (3,942,400 pixels) and all ten walking frames (563,200 pixels),
with zero mismatches. The published diagnostic has not
been replaced. No emulator GUI was used.
